Uncertainty Relations for Angular Momentum

Lars Dammeier Email: lars.dammeier@itp.uni-hannover.de Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Leibniz Universität, Hannover, Germany    René Schwonnek Email: rene.schwonnek@itp.uni-hannover.de Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Leibniz Universität, Hannover, Germany    Reinhard F. Werner Email: reinhard.werner@itp.uni-hannover.de Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik, Leibniz Universität, Hannover, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

In this work we study various notions of uncertainty for angular momentum in the spin-ss representation of S​U​(2)SU(2). We characterize the “uncertainty regions” given by all vectors, whose components are specified by the variances of the three angular momentum components. A basic feature of this set is a lower bound for the sum of the three variances. We give a method for obtaining optimal lower bounds for uncertainty regions for general operator triples, and evaluate these for small ss. Further lower bounds are derived by generalizing the technique by which Robertson obtained his state-dependent lower bound. These are optimal for large ss, since they are saturated by states taken from the Holstein-Primakoff approximation. We show that, for all ss, all variances are consistent with the so-called vector model, i.e., they can also be realized by a classical probability measure on a sphere of radius s⁡(s+1)\sqrt{s(s+1)}. Entropic uncertainty relations can be discussed similarly, but are minimized by different states than those minimizing the variances for small ss. For large ss the Maassen-Uffink bound becomes sharp and we explicitly describe the extremalizing states.

Measurement uncertainty, as recently discussed by Busch, Lahti and Werner for position and momentum, is introduced and a generalized observable (POVM) which minimizes the worst case measurement uncertainty of all angular momentum components is explicitly determined, along with the minimal uncertainty. The output vectors for the optimal measurement all have the same length r⁡(s)r(s), where r⁡(s)/s→1r(s)/s\to 1 as s→∞s\to\infty.

I Introduction

The textbook literature on quantum mechanics seems to agree that the uncertainty relations for angular momentum, and indeed for any pair of quantum observables A,BA,B should be given by Robertson’s [26] inequality

Δρ2​(A)​Δρ2​(B)≥14​(trρ​i​[A,B])2,\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(B)\geq\frac{1}{4}(\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho\,i[A,B])^{2}, (1)

valid for any density operator ρ\rho, with Δρ2​(A)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A) denoting the variance of the outcomes of a measurement of AA on the state ρ\rho. Perhaps the main reason for the ubiquity of this relation in textbooks is that it is such a convenient intermediate step to the proof of uncertainty relations for position and momentum. In that case the right hand side is ℏ2/4\hbar^{2}/4, independently of the state ρ\rho. For any pair A,BA,B other than a canonical pair, however, the relation (1) makes a much weaker statement, requiring some prior information about the state. This begs the question: When and with what bounds it is true that

[Preparation Uncertainty:]
One cannot choose a state ρ\rho so that Δρ2​(A)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A) and Δρ2​(B)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(B) simultaneously become arbitrarily small.

Robertson’s relation supports no such conclusion, but on the other hand such a statement does hold in many situations. In fact, in a finite dimensional context it is true whenever AA and BB do not have a common eigenvector. In this paper we will provide optimal bounds for angular momentum components, establishing the methods for deriving optimal bounds in the general case along the way.

The second reason that (1) is unsatisfactory is that it addresses only the preparation side of uncertainty, in the sense loosely described in the italicized sentence above. However, there is always also a measurement aspect to uncertainty, for which Heisenberg’s γ\gamma-ray microscope [9] is a paradigm. The error disturbance tradeoff would be stated as

[Error-Disturbance Uncertainty:]
An approximate measurement of AA of accuracy Δ​A\Delta A disturbs the system in such a way that from the post-measurement state and the measurement result for AA the distribution for observable BB can only be inferred with accuracy Δ​B\Delta B, where Δ​A\Delta A and Δ​B\Delta B cannot be simultaneously arbitrarily small.

It is often easier to think of the whole experiment as a joint measurement of AA and BB, and state relations of the kind:

[Measurement Uncertainty:]
For any measurement device with both an AA- type and a BB-type output, the marginals will have worst case error Δ​A\Delta A, Δ​B\Delta B with respect to ideal measurements of AA and BB, satisfying a tradeoff relation.

Again, generic observables and angular momenta satisfy non-trivial relations of this kind. Errors Δ​A=Δ​B=0\Delta A=\Delta B=0 can occur only if AA and BB commute, i.e., under an even more stringent condition than for preparation uncertainty. In this paper we will provide some sharp measurement uncertainty relations for angular momentum, establishing along the way some methods which may be of interest in more general cases.

There is a third reason that one should not be satisfied with (1) with A=L1,B=L2A=L_{1},\ B=L_{2}: It involves only two of the three components of angular momentum. But there is no reason tradeoff-relations as described above should not be stated for more than two observables. For angular momentum this seems especially natural. Moreover, it seems natural to state relations for all components simultaneously, i.e., not only for the three components along the axes of an arbitrarily chosen Cartesian reference frame, but for the angular momenta along arbitrary rotation axes, restoring the rotational symmetry of the problem.

Indeed the idea that uncertainty should involve just pairs of observables can be traced to Bohr’s habit of expressing complementarity as a relation between “opposite” aspects, like ‘in vitro’ and ‘in vivo’ biology. This dualistic preference had more to do with his philosophy than with the actual structure of quantum mechanics. Other founding fathers of quantum mechanics did not share this preference. As Wigner said in an interview [35] in 1963:

I always felt also that this duality is not solved and in this I may have been under Johnny’s [John von Neumann] influence, who said, “Well, there are many things which do not commute and you can easily find three operators which do not commute.” I also was very much under the influence of the spin where you have three variables which are entirely, so to speak, symmetric within themselves and clearly show that it isn’t two that are complementary; and I still don’t feel that this duality is a terribly significant and striking property of the concepts.

In this spirit, an uncertainty relation for triples of canonical operators was recently proposed and proved [17], and further generalizations are clearly possible. However, we will stick to angular momentum in this paper, and particularly seek to establish relations which do not break rotation invariance.

Our paper responds to an increasing interest in quantitative uncertainty relations. This interest is connected to an increasing number of experiments reaching the uncertainty dominated regime, so that that rather than qualitative or order-of-magnitude statements one is more interested in the precise location of the quantum limits. Measurement uncertainty was made rigorous in [3, 5, 27]. There is also a controversial [6, 4] state-dependent version [23]. That adequate uncertainty relations are sometimes better stated in terms of the sum of variances rather than their product has been noted repeatedly [11, 15, 21]. There has been some renewed interest also in the uncertainty between angular momentum and angular position [8], angular momentum of certain states [25] and other non-standard complementary pairs [19].

I.1 Setting and notation

In physics angular momentum appears as orbital or as spin angular momentum. Our theory applies to both, but it must be noted that the bounds obtained do depend on the quantum number for 𝐋2{\mathbf{L}}^{2}. For example, there are states with vanishing orbital angular momentum uncertainties (precisely the rotation invariant ones, i.e., s=0s=0) but none for a s=12s=\frac{1}{2} degree of freedom. Therefore, one first has to decompose the given space into irreducible angular momentum components (integer or half integer), and then use the results for the appropriate ss. Hence we will consider throughout a system of spin ss, with s=1/2,1,3/2,…s=1/2,1,3/2,... in its (2​s+1)(2s+1)-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ=ℂ2​s+1{\mathcal{H}}={\mathbb{C}}^{2s+1}. The three angular momentum components will be denoted by LkL_{k}, k=1,2,3k=1,2,3, and the component along a unit vector 𝐞∈ℝ3{\mathbf{e}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} by 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}. We denote by |m⟩|m\rangle the eigenvectors of L3L_{3}, so that L3​|m⟩=m​|m⟩L_{3}|m\rangle=m|m\rangle where −s≤m≤s-s\leq m\leq s and, with L±=L1±i​L2L_{\pm}=L_{1}\pm iL_{2},

L±​|m⟩=s⁡(s+1)−m⁡(m±1)​|m±1⟩.L_{\pm}|m\rangle=\sqrt{s(s+1)-m(m\pm 1)}|m\pm 1\rangle. (2)

Rotation matrices, whether they are considered as elements of SO(3) or of SU(2), will typically be denoted by RR, the corresponding matrix in the spin ss representation by URU_{R}, and normalized Haar measure on SO(3) or SU(2) by d​RdR. We will always set ℏ=1\hbar=1. Observables are in general always allowed to be normalized positive operator valued measures (POVMs), with a typical letter FF. For a self-adjoint operator AA the spectral measure is an observable in this sense, denoted by EAE_{A}. For a component of angular momentum, i.e., A=𝐞⋅𝐋A={{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}} we write E𝐞E_{\mathbf{e}} for short. For the unit vectors 𝐞k{\mathbf{e}}_{k} along the axes we further abbreviate this to EkE_{k}.

For the variance of the probability distribution obtained by measuring FF on a state (density operator) ρ\rho we write

Δρ2​(F)=min⁡∫ξ⁡(x−ξ)2​trρ​F​(𝑑x).\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(F)=\min_{\xi}\int(x-\xi)^{2}\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho F(dx). (3)

This minimum is taken over a quadratic expression in ξ\xi, and it is attained when ξ=∫x​trρ​F​(𝑑x)\xi=\int x\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho F(dx) is the mean value of the distribution. The most familiar case is that of the spectral measure for an operator AA, in which case we abbreviate the variance by Δρ2​(A)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A). Then the second moment ∫x2​trρ​F​(𝑑x)=A2\int x^{2}\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho F(dx)=A^{2} can also be expressed by AA and we get

Δρ2​(A)=Δρ2​(EA)=tr(ρ​A2)−tr(ρ​A)2.\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A)=\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(E_{A})=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits(\rho A^{2})-\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits(\rho A)^{2}. (4)

We say that a unit vector |ϕ⟩∈ℋ|\phi\rangle\in{\mathcal{H}} is a maximal weight vector, if for some direction 𝐞∈ℝ3{\mathbf{e}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} it satisfies 𝐞⋅𝐋​|ϕ⟩=s​|ϕ⟩{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}|\phi\rangle=s|\phi\rangle. This is the same as saying that, for some rotation R∈R\inSU(2), |ϕ⟩=UR​|s⟩|\phi\rangle=U_{R}|s\rangle up to a phase. For such a vector we call ρ=|ϕ⟩​⟨ϕ|\rho={|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|} a spin coherent state. These states are candidates for states of minimal uncertainty.

I.2 Summary of Main Results

We now describe the structure of our paper and the main results.

Sect. II: Preparation uncertainty. — The basic object of study is the variance Δρ2​(𝐞⋅𝐋)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}) of the angular momentum in direction 𝐞{\mathbf{e}} as a function of the unit vector 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}, especially properties which hold for an arbitrary state ρ\rho. After clarifying some general features and explicitly solving the two cases s≤1s\leq 1 (Sect. II.2), we look at the traditional setting of just two components L1,L2L_{1},L_{2}. The set of uncertainty pairs (Δρ2​(L1),Δρ2​(L2))\bigl(\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{1}),\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{2})\bigr) is studied, and the fact that not both variances can be small is found to be well expressed by a lower bound not on the product but on the sum of the variances. We compute numerically (and exactly up to s=3/2s=3/2) the best constants in

Δρ2​(L1)+Δρ2​(L3)≥c2​(s)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{1})+\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{3})\geq c_{2}(s) (5)

and find that they asymptotically behave like c2​(s)∼s2/3c_{2}(s)\sim s^{2/3} (Sect. II.4). For three components the uncertainty region is also studied in some detail. A prominent feature is again given by a linear bound [11]

Δρ2​(L1)+Δρ2​(L2)+Δρ2​(L3)≥s,\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{1})+\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{2})+\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{3})\geq s, (6)

which is very easy to prove (see Sect. II.1, (17)).

Turning to features of the whole function 𝐞↦Δρ2​(𝐞⋅𝐋){\mathbf{e}}\mapsto\Delta^{2}_{\rho}({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}), we show in Sect. II.5 that for any ρ\rho there is at least one direction 𝐞{\mathbf{e}} such that Δρ2​(𝐞⋅𝐋)≥s/2\Delta^{2}_{\rho}({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}})\geq s/2, i.e.,

max𝐞⁡Δρ2​(𝐞⋅𝐋)≥s2.\max_{\mathbf{e}}\Delta^{2}_{\rho}({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}})\geq\frac{s}{2}. (7)

This bound is optimal, since it is saturated by spin coherent states. We generalize from the maximum (seen as the L∞L^{\infty}-norm) to all LpL^{p}-norms (Prop. 1).

For large ss Eq. (6) suggests the scaling ∼1/s\sim 1/s (Sect. II.7). Indeed, the triples (Δρ2​(L1)/s,Δρ2​(L2)/s,Δρ2​(L3)/s)(\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{1})/s,\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{2})/s,\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{3})/s) converge as s→∞s\to\infty (Theorem 4). The lower bound on the limit set is obtained by a generalization of Robertson’s method for proving (1) Sect. II.6, which for finite ss is (39)

Δρ2​(L1)​(Δρ2​(L2)+Δρ2​(L3))≥14​(s⁡(s+1)−Δρ2​(L1)−Δρ2​(L2)−Δρ2​(L3)),\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{1})\Bigl(\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{2})+\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{3})\Bigr)\geq\frac{1}{4}\Bigl(s(s+1)-\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{1})-\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{2})-\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{3})\Bigr), (8)

where the components are ordered so that Δρ2​(L1)≥Δρ2​(L2)≥Δρ2​(L3)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{1})\geq\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{2})\geq\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{3}). The upper bound in Theorem 4 is provided by a family of states suggested by the Holstein-Primakoff approximation.

Sect. III.1: Vector model and moment problems. — We revisit the so-called vector model of angular momentum, a classical model which is still found in some textbooks. We show that it can correctly portray the moments up to second order (i.e., means and variances) of the angular momentum observables, but fails on higher moments and, of course, on correlations.

Sect. III.2: Entropic uncertainty relations. — We discuss entropic uncertainty relations only very briefly. We point out that the criteria “variance” and “entropy” may disagree on which of two distributions is “more sharply concentrated”. This effect is illustrated by the uncertainty diagrams for s=1s=1. We show also that the general Maassen-Uffink bound [20] while suboptimal for s=1s=1, becomes sharp for s→∞s\to\infty, and determine a family of states saturating it.

Sect. IV: Measurement uncertainty. — We consider two measures for the deviation of an approximate observable from an ideal reference, called metric error and calibration error. We then discuss uncertainty relations for the joint measurement of all angular momentum components. The output of such an observable is an angular momentum 3-vector 𝜼{\boldsymbol{\eta}}, from which one can obtain a measurement of the 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}-component (for any unit vector 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}) simply by taking 𝐞⋅𝜼{\mathbf{e}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\eta}} as the output. Such a marginal observable can in turn be compared with the quantum observable 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}. The uncertainty relation in this case gives a lower bound on the error in the worst case with respect to 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}. Our main result (Theorem 12) is a determination of the optimal bound, and an observable saturating it. It turns out that the optimal observable is covariant with respect to rotations, and this implies that it simultaneously minimizes the maximal metric error and the maximal calibration error. All the output vectors have the same length rmin​(s)r_{\rm min}(s), which depends in a non-trivial way on ss but is close to ss for large ss.

II Preparation Uncertainty

In this section we consider the preparation uncertainty, i.e., a property of a given state ρ\rho. For every unit vector 𝐞∈ℝ3{\mathbf{e}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} we can form the variance of the angular momentum component 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}, and hence study the function

v(𝐞)=Δρ2(𝐞⋅𝐋)=tr(ρ(𝐞⋅𝐋)2)−(trρ𝐞⋅𝐋)2v({\mathbf{e}})=\Delta^{2}_{\rho}({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}})=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\Bigr(\rho({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}})^{2}\Bigl)-\Bigr(\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho\,{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}\Bigl)^{2} (9)

on the unit sphere. For the purposes of this section, this function summarizes all the uncertainty properties of the state ρ\rho, and all results in this section are statements about properties of this function, which are valid for all ρ\rho. To visualize the function vv, we can use a three-dimensional radial plot, i.e., the surface containing all vectors v⁡(𝐞)​𝐞v({\mathbf{e}}){\mathbf{e}}, as 𝐞{\mathbf{e}} runs over all unit vectors. A typical radial plot is shown in FIG. 1. Often we are also interested in the components with respect to some Cartesian reference frame. In this case the best visualization is an uncertainty diagram, which represents the possible pairs/triples etc. of variances in the same state. In our case this will be the set of pairs (v⁡(𝐞1),v⁡(𝐞2))(v({\mathbf{e}}_{1}),v({\mathbf{e}}_{2})), or triples (v⁡(𝐞1),v⁡(𝐞2),v⁡(𝐞3))(v({\mathbf{e}}_{1}),v({\mathbf{e}}_{2}),v({\mathbf{e}}_{3})). The diagrams for s=1s=1 are shown in FIG. 4. In this diagram it can be seen that the uncertainty region is not convex in general. Since we are only interested in lower bounds, we therefore always take the monotone closure of the uncertainty region, i.e., we also include with every point the whole quadrant/octant of points in which one or more of the coordinates increase. This is described in more detail in Sect. II.3.

It turns out that after a rotation to suitable principal axes (which has already been carried out in FIG. 1), the function vv depends only on three real parameters μ1,μ2,μ3\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}. To see this we introduce the 3×33\times 3-matrix Λ=Λ⁡(ρ)\Lambda=\Lambda(\rho) by

v⁡(𝐞)\displaystyle v({\mathbf{e}}) =\displaystyle= ∑j​kej​ek​Λj​k​(ρ)with\displaystyle\sum_{jk}e_{j}e_{k}\ \Lambda_{jk}(\rho)\qquad\mbox{with} (10)
Λj​k​(ρ)\displaystyle\Lambda_{jk}(\rho) =\displaystyle= ℜ⁡e​tr(ρ​Lj​Lk)−λj​λk\displaystyle\Re e\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits(\rho L_{j}L_{k})-\lambda_{j}\lambda_{k} (11)
λj​(ρ)\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(\rho) =\displaystyle= tr(ρ​Lj).\displaystyle\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits(\rho L_{j}). (12)

Since the LkL_{k} transform as a vector operator (i.e., with respect to the spin-1 representation of SU(2)) we see that by choice of an appropriate coordinate basis in ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3} we can diagonalize Λ\Lambda, i.e., we can choose Λj​k​(ρ)=μj​δj​k\Lambda_{jk}(\rho)=\mu_{j}\delta_{jk} with μ1≥μ2≥μ3≥0\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\mu_{3}\geq 0.

The eigenvalues (μ1,μ2,μ3)(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}) of any matrix Λ⁡(ρ)\Lambda(\rho) are also a possible triple of variances, namely for a suitably rotated state. In fact, we can find the uncertainty triples for all rotated versions of ρ\rho quite easily: When RR is the rotation matrix taking the eigenbasis of Λ\Lambda to the basis 𝐞1,𝐞2,𝐞3{\mathbf{e}}_{1},{\mathbf{e}}_{2},{\mathbf{e}}_{3} under consideration, then

v⁡(𝐞j)=∑kRj​k2​μk.v({\mathbf{e}}_{j})=\sum_{k}R_{jk}^{2}\mu_{k}. (13)

Now the squared rotation matrix is doubly stochastic, so by Birkhoff’s theorem it is a convex combination of permutation matrices. We therefore find the variance triple in basis 𝐞{\mathbf{e}} in the convex hull of the six points, arising from the triple of μk\mu_{k} by permutation. These six points lie in a plane orthogonal to the vector (1,1,1)(1,1,1), so they form a hexagon (see FIG. 2), which degenerates into a triangle if two of the μk\mu_{k} are equal. One can easily check that the full hexagon is attained by squared rotation matrices.

II.1 Basic bounds

For an L3L_{3}-eigenstate ρ=|m⟩​⟨m|\rho={|m\rangle\langle m|} we find λ=(0,0,m)\lambda=(0,0,m) and

Λ⁡(|m⟩​⟨m|)=12​(s⁡(s+1)−m2)​(100010000)≥s2​(100010000),\Lambda({|m\rangle\langle m|})=\frac{1}{2}(s(s+1)-m^{2})\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\geq\frac{s}{2}\,\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}, (14)

which re-inforces that, for eigenstates, the variances in all directions are smallest for the maximal weight m=sm=s. Maximal variance is attained for an equal weight mixture ρ=1/2​(|s⟩​⟨s|+|−s⟩​⟨−s|)\rho=1/2\bigl({|s\rangle\langle s|}+{|-s\rangle\langle-s|}\bigr), which has L3L_{3}-variance s2s^{2}. Hence, for all 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}:

0≤v⁡(𝐞)≤s2.0\leq v({\mathbf{e}})\leq s^{2}. (15)

The average v⁡(𝐞)¯\overline{v({\mathbf{e}})} over 𝐞{\mathbf{e}} with respect to the surface measure on the sphere, or equivalently the average of v⁡(R​𝐞)v(R{\mathbf{e}}) over Haar-random rotations RR, is readily computed from (10), since the average of ej​eke_{j}e_{k} over the unit sphere is just δj​k/3\delta_{jk}/3. Therefore, from (10),

v⁡(𝐞)¯=13​trΛ⁡(ρ)=13​(s⁡(s+1)−|𝝀|2)≥13​(s⁡(s+1)−s2)≥s3.\overline{v({\mathbf{e}})}=\frac{1}{3}\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\Lambda(\rho)=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(s(s+1)-|{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}|^{2}\bigr)\geq\frac{1}{3}\bigl(s(s+1)-s^{2}\bigr)\geq\frac{s}{3}. (16)

In the same simple way we can get an inequality for the variances along the three coordinate directions of a Cartesian coordinate system:

∑k=13v⁡(𝐞k)=trΛ⁡(ρ)≥s.\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{3}v({\mathbf{e}}_{k})=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\Lambda(\rho)\geq s. (17)

In both cases equality holds precisely for |𝝀|=s|{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}|=s, i.e., if ρ\rho is an eigenstate of one of the operators 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}} for the maximum eigenvalue m=sm=s.

II.2 Special features for s=1/2s=1/2 and s=1s=1

For s=1/2s=1/2, it happens that LjL_{j} and LkL_{k} (i.e., up to a factor the Pauli matrices) anticommute for different j,kj,k, so that

s=12:Λj​k​(ρ)=14​δj​k−λj​λk.s=\frac{1}{2}:\qquad\Lambda_{jk}(\rho)=\frac{1}{4}\delta_{jk}-\lambda_{j}\lambda_{k}. (18)

The eigenvalues are (μ1,μ2,μ3)=1/4​(1,1,1−4​|λ|2)(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3})=1/4(1,1,1-4|\lambda|^{2}). Of course, pure states are characterized by |𝝀|=12|{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}|=\frac{1}{2}. The uncertainties are 1/4−λj21/4-\lambda_{j}^{2}, and so the uncertainty region is described by a triangle.

The case s=1s=1 is still special because the 3+63+6 operators LkL_{k} and (Lj​Lk+Lk​Lj)/2(L_{j}L_{k}+L_{k}L_{j})/2 form a basis of the operators on ℂ3{\mathbb{C}}^{3}. Therefore, ρ\rho can be reconstructed from (𝝀,Λ)({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},\Lambda) and, in particular, the set of pure ρ\rho can be characterized in terms of conditions on the eigenvalues μk\mu_{k} and λk\lambda_{k}. In order to analyze these conditions, let us take the representation of the group SU(2) by real orthogonal matrices. Now consider a vector ψ∈ℂ3\psi\in{\mathbb{C}}^{3}, which we can split into ψ=ℜ⁡e​ψ+i​ℑ​m​ψ\psi=\Re e\psi+i\,\Im m\psi with ℜ⁡e​ψ,ℑ⁡m​ψ∈ℝ3\Re e\psi,\Im m\psi\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. Note that the real continuous function t↦⟨ℜ⁡e⁡(ei​t​ψ),ℑ⁡m⁡(ei​t​ψ)⟩t\mapsto\left\langle\Re e\bigl(e^{it}\psi\bigr),\Im m\bigl(e^{it}\psi\bigr)\right\rangle changes sign between t=0t=0 and t=π/2t=\pi/2, so we can choose a complex phase for ψ\psi to make ℜ⁡e​ψ\Re e\psi and ℑ⁡m​ψ\Im m\psi orthogonal. Moreover, we can apply a rotation, so that ℜ⁡e​ψ\Re e\psi and ℑ⁡m​ψ\Im m\psi are along the first two coordinate axes. Hence, up to a rotation, we have

where t∈[−π,π]t\in[-\pi,\pi] or τ=(sin⁡t)2∈[0,1]\tau=(\sin t)^{2}\in[0,1]. In the three-component diagram the curve parameterized by τ\tau is a parabola lying in a diagonal plane. This parabola, and the two copies arising by coordinate permutation are shown in FIG. 3, as well as the body of uncertainty triples of all pure states, which arises by adding to each point on the parabola the hexagon formed by its permutation orbit. A paper cutout model of this solid is provided as a supplement [1].

II.3 General minimization method

Consider now, a little more generally, any collection of hermitian operators A1,…,AnA_{1},\ldots,A_{n}. We can then form, for any state ρ\rho, the variance nn-tuple (Δρ2​(A1),…,Δρ2​(An))(\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A_{1}),\ldots,\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A_{n})), and ask which region Ω\Omega in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} is filled, when ρ\rho runs over the whole state space. We call Ω\Omega the uncertainty region of the operator tuple. Typically, this is not a convex set, because Δρ2​(A)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A) contains a term quadratic in ρ\rho, which consequently does not respect convex mixtures. Ω\Omega will be simply connected (as a continuous image of the state space), but beyond that there are few general facts. It can happen that starting from a point in the uncertainty region we can leave the region by increasing one of the coordinates, i.e., the region encodes upper bounds on variances as well as lower bounds. This is clearly not relevant to the theme of uncertainty relations, where we ask for universal lower bounds only. We can therefore consider the monotone closure of the uncertainty region, by including all points with larger uncertainties, i.e.,

Ω+={(x1,…,xn)|∃ρ​∀α​xα≥Δρ2​(Aα)}.\Omega^{+}=\bigl\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\bigm|\exists\rho\ \forall\alpha\ x_{\alpha}\geq\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A_{\alpha})\bigr\}. (20)

This is still not necessarily a convex set. We will denote the convex hull of Ω+\Omega^{+} by Ω∨\Omega^{\vee} and call it the lower convex hull of Ω\Omega (see FIG. 4). It is this set which has an efficient characterization. Indeed, as a closed convex set it is the intersection of all half spaces containing it, and the monotonicity condition restricts these half spaces to those whose normal vector ww has all components non-negative. In other words,

Ω∨\displaystyle\Omega^{\vee} =\displaystyle= {(x1,…,xn)|∀wα≥0:∑αwαxα≥m(w1,…,wn)},\displaystyle\bigl\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\bigm|\forall w_{\alpha}\geq 0:\ \sum_{\alpha}w_{\alpha}x_{\alpha}\geq m(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n})\bigr\}, (21)
m⁡(w1,…,wn)\displaystyle m(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}) =\displaystyle= infρ∑αwα​Δρ2​(Aα)\displaystyle\inf_{\rho}\ \sum_{\alpha}w_{\alpha}\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(A_{\alpha}) (22)
=\displaystyle= infρinfa1,…,an∑αwα​trρ​(Aα−aα​1​I)2\displaystyle\inf_{\rho}\ \inf_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}}\ \sum_{\alpha}w_{\alpha}\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho\bigl(A_{\alpha}-a_{\alpha}{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}\bigr)^{2}

In this double infimum we can exchange the order, leading to two kinds of operations: With fixed ρ\rho the global minimum over the aαa_{\alpha} is obviously at aα=trρ​Aαa_{\alpha}=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho A_{\alpha}. On the other hand, with fixed aαa_{\alpha} the global minimum over ρ\rho is computed by finding the ground state of the positive semidefinite operator H⁡(a)=∑αwα​(Aα−aα​1​I)2H(a)=\sum_{\alpha}w_{\alpha}\bigl(A_{\alpha}-a_{\alpha}{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}\bigr)^{2}. An efficient algorithm is therefore obtained by alternating between these two steps. The upper estimates on mm obtained in this way are non-increasing and in practice converge quite well, and independently of the starting value. However, we do not have a theorem to this effect. An analytic consequence of this algorithm (independent of convergence) is that we can restrict the infimum to pure states, since this is sufficient to get the ground state energies.

The algorithm is then run for a suitable set of tuples (w1,…,wn)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}), so that for each run, one obtains a tangent plane to Ω∨\Omega^{\vee} but also the state ρ\rho and with it, the tuple of variances in Ω\Omega. We illustrate the results in FIG. 4 for the case of spin 1, and the operator tuples (L1,L2)(L_{1},L_{2}) and (L1,L2,L3)(L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}), respectively. For low spin these diagrams can be determined analytically (see the next subsection). The most prominent feature of two-component diagram is the symmetric linear bound, which depends on ss and is determined in subsection II.4.

II.5 Power mean and maximal uncertainty

A natural way to characterize states with small variance is to look for the maximum of the variance function v⁡(𝐞)v({\mathbf{e}}) defined in (10). An uncertainty relation would then put a lower bound c⁡(s)c(s) on this maximum. In other words we would like to prove the following statement: For every state ρ\rho there is some direction ee such that Δρ2​(Ee)\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(E_{e}) is larger than cc. By considering coherent states we can immediately see that c⁡(s)≤s/2c(s)\leq s/2. The following proposition shows that coherent states in fact have minimal variance in terms of this criterion, and we even have equality.

Such a result can be seen as one end of a one-parameter family of criteria, of which (16) is the other end: We can judge the “size” of the function vv by its ℒp{\cal L}^{p} norm, of which the maximum is the special case p=∞p=\infty, and the mean the case p=1p=1. We therefore formulate a proposition to cover all these cases.

Proposition 1.

For every s∈ℕ/2s\in{\mathbb{N}}/2 and every p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty] there is a constant c⁡(p,s)c(p,s) such that, for every density operator ρ\rho in the spin ss representation,

‖v‖p=(∫d​e4​π​Δρp​(𝐞⋅𝐋))1p≥c⁡(p,s)\left\|v\right\|_{p}=\left(\!\int\frac{de}{4\pi}\ \Delta^{p}_{\rho}({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}})\right)^{\textstyle\frac{1}{p}}\geq c(p,s) (29)

with equality whenever ρ\rho is a spin coherent state. For p<∞p<\infty these are the only states with equality. The constant is

with special values c⁡(1,s)=s/3c(1,s)=s/3, c⁡(2,s)=s​8/15≈0.73​sc(2,s)=s\sqrt{8/15}\approx 0.73s, c⁡(∞,s)=s/2c(\infty,s)=s/2.

Proof.

Let λj=trρ​Lj\lambda_{j}=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho L_{j} be the vector of expectation values, and consider the set of density operators ρβ\rho^{\beta} arising from ρ\rho by rotation RβR_{\beta} around the vector λ\lambda by the angle β\beta. For each ρβ\rho^{\beta}, we call the variance function vβ​(𝐞)=v⁡(Rβ​𝐞)v_{\beta}(\mathbf{e})=v(R_{\beta}\mathbf{e}). By averaging over β\beta we find a state ρ¯\overline{\rho}, with variance function

where we used, crucially, that all ρβ\rho^{\beta} and ρ¯\overline{\rho} have the same expectations λj\lambda_{j}. II.6 Robertson’s technique: a generalization

We have criticized the Robertson inequality (1) for not giving a state independent bound. However, with only little effort it can be used to derive such a bound. Indeed, abbreviating vj=Δρ2​(Lj)v_{j}=\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{j}), and λj=trρ​Lj\lambda_{j}=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho L_{j} we can add the three inequalities of the form v1​v2≥λ32/4v_{1}v_{2}\geq\lambda_{3}^{2}/4 and use that ∑j(vj+λj2)=s⁡(s+1)\sum_{j}(v_{j}+\lambda_{j}^{2})=s(s+1) to obtain

v1​v2+v2​v3+v3​v1≥14​(s⁡(s+1)−(v1+v2+v3)).v_{1}v_{2}+v_{2}v_{3}+v_{3}v_{1}\geq\frac{1}{4}\bigl(s(s+1)-(v_{1}+v_{2}+v_{3})\bigr). (36)

Clearly, this no longer allows v1=v2=0v_{1}=v_{2}=0, since v3≤s2v_{3}\leq s^{2}. The set of variance triples satisfying this is shown in FIG. 6. Comparison with FIG.4 readily shows that this bound is not optimal. However, we can generalize Robertson’s technique from two to three components rather than extend his two component result in this trivial way. The basis of the technique is to utilize the observation that for any finite collection of operators XjX_{j} (not necessarily hermitian or normal) the matrix mj​k=trρ​Xj∗​Xkm_{jk}=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho X_{j}^{*}X_{k} is positive definite, which is the same as saying that for any complex linear combination X=∑jaj​XjX=\sum_{j}a_{j}X_{j} the expectation of X∗​XX^{*}X must be positive. In order to get Robertson’s inequality for L1,L2L_{1},L_{2} this idea is applied to the three operators 1​I,L1,L2{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI},L_{1},L_{2}. In fact, this leads to Schrödinger’s improvement of the inequality [28] which also contains the square of the covariance matrix element Λ12​(ρ)2\Lambda_{12}(\rho)^{2} on the right hand side.

We will apply the method to the four operators 1​I,L1,L2,L3{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI},L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}. In order to simplify the expressions, however, we will not look for variances and the off-diagonal elements of Λ⁡(ρ)\Lambda(\rho), but for inequalities involving the eigenvalues μj\mu_{j}. As discussed at the beginning of this section, this will contain all the information needed. In other words, we will take the matrix Λ⁡(ρ)\Lambda(\rho) as the diagonal matrix with entries μ1≥μ2≥μ2\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\mu_{2}. The matrix which then needs to be positive is

M=(1λ1λ2λ3λ1μ1+λ12λ1​λ2+i​λ3/2λ1​λ3−i​λ2/2λ2λ1​λ2−i​λ3/2μ2+λ22λ2​λ3+i​λ1/2λ3λ1​λ3+i​λ2/2λ2​λ3−i​λ1/2μ3+λ32).M=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}1&\lambda_{1}&\lambda_{2}&\lambda_{3}\\[3.0pt] \lambda_{1}&\mu_{1}+\lambda_{1}^{2}&\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}+i\lambda_{3}/2&\lambda_{1}\lambda_{3}-i\lambda_{2}/2\\[3.0pt] \lambda_{2}&\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}-i\lambda_{3}/2&\mu_{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}&\lambda_{2}\lambda_{3}+i\lambda_{1}/2\\[3.0pt] \lambda_{3}&\lambda_{1}\lambda_{3}+i\lambda_{2}/2&\lambda_{2}\lambda_{3}-i\lambda_{1}/2&\mu_{3}+\lambda_{3}^{2}\end{array}\right). (37)

The positivity of this matrix is equivalent (see e.g. [14, Thm. 7.2.5]) to the positivity of the principal minors, i.e., the determinants of the submatrices of the first kk rows and columns for k=1,2,3,4k=1,2,3,4. The first three of these are 11, μ1\mu_{1}, and μ1​μ2−λ32/4\mu_{1}\mu_{2}-\lambda_{3}^{2}/4. The positivity of the third one is Robertson’s inequality (1). The only remaining condition for the positivity of MM is detM≥0\det M\geq 0, which evaluates to

μ1​μ2​μ3−14​(λ12​μ1+λ22​μ2+λ32​μ3)≥0.\mu_{1}\mu_{2}\mu_{3}-\frac{1}{4}\bigl(\lambda_{1}^{2}\mu_{1}+\lambda_{2}^{2}\mu_{2}+\lambda_{3}^{2}\mu_{3}\bigr)\geq 0. (38)

This will be combined with the normalization condition

λ12+λ22+λ32=s⁡(s+1)−(μ1+μ2+μ3).\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{3}^{2}=s(s+1)-(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}+\mu_{3}). (39)

The condition on the triples (μ1,μ2,μ3)(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}) we have to evaluate is the existence of λi\lambda_{i} satisfying both these relations. Since only the squares enter, let us set xj=λj2x_{j}=\lambda_{j}^{2}. Then (39) describes a triangle in the positive quadrant with equal intercept s⁡(s+1)−(μ1+μ2+μ3)s(s+1)-(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}+\mu_{3}) with the axes. The inequality (38) describes a tetrahedron spanned by the origin and the axis intercepts x10=4​μ2​μ3x_{1}^{0}=4\mu_{2}\mu_{3}, and cyclic. Note that Robertson’s inequality is automatically satisfied on this tetrahedron. Obviously the tetrahedron and the triangle intersect if an only if one of the axis intercepts of the tetrahedron reaches or lies above the triangle. Since we can take the eigenvalues ordered: μ1≥μ2≥μ3\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\mu_{3} this means

4​μ1​μ2≥s⁡(s+1)−(μ1+μ2+μ3).4\mu_{1}\mu_{2}\geq s(s+1)-(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}+\mu_{3}). (40)

This is a bound to the eigenvalue of the Λ\Lambda-matrix. By Birkhoffs theorem, the variances arising from such Λ\Lambda also includes all convex combinations of permutations of the μi\mu_{i} (see beginning of Sect. II). In order to characterize the set of variance triples generated in this way we need the following Lemma. In its formulation the variables σ∈S3\sigma\in S_{3} run over the permutation group on three elements, and are applied to the components of a 3-vector (see also FIG. 2).

II.7 Asymptotic Case

Now we take a look at the behavior of the asymptotic uncertainty region for s→∞s\to\infty. We already know that Δρ2​(L1)+Δρ2​(L2)+Δρ2​(L3)≥s\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{1})+\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{2})+\Delta^{2}_{\rho}(L_{3})\geq s and hence it is appropriate to scale the problem by 1/ss, which will fix the sum of the variance in the lower base triangle to 11. We start with the asymptotic behavior of the generalized Robertson inequality derived in the previous section. On the scale of 1/s1/s, i.e. vi/s=νi{v_{i}}/{s}=\nu_{i}, and the ordering ν1≥ν2≥ν3\nu_{1}\geq\nu_{2}\geq\nu_{3} this inequality reads

4​ν1​(ν2+ν3)≥1+1s​(1−(ν1+ν2+ν3))4\nu_{1}(\nu_{2}+\nu_{3})\geq 1+\frac{1}{s}(1-(\nu_{1}+\nu_{2}+\nu_{3})) (48)

and as ss goes to infinity the set of possible variances shrink to

4​ν1​(ν2+ν3)≥1,4\nu_{1}(\nu_{2}+\nu_{3})\geq 1, (49)

because ∑iνi≥1\sum_{i}\nu_{i}\geq 1. Hence the inequality (48) gets stronger for increasing ss.

In this section we will show that this bound is attained by states, which will be constructed in the following way. Using the technique described in part II.3, we look for the states ψ\psi, which minimize the expectation of the operator

H⁡(s,𝐰)=1s​(w1​(L1−λ1)2+w2​(L2−λ2)2+w3​(L3−λ3)2),H(s,\mathbf{w})=\frac{1}{s}\Big(w_{1}(L_{1}-\lambda_{1})^{2}+w_{2}(L_{2}-\lambda_{2})^{2}+w_{3}(L_{3}-\lambda_{3})^{2}\Big), (50)

for a normal vector 𝐰\mathbf{w}. We do this using the Holstein Primakoff transformation [12]:

L+=2​s​1−a∗​a2​s​aL−=2​s​a∗​1−a∗​a2​sL3=s−a∗​a.L_{+}=\sqrt{2s}\sqrt{1-\frac{a^{*}a}{2s}}a\quad L_{-}=\sqrt{2s}a^{*}\sqrt{1-\frac{a^{*}a}{2s}}\quad L_{3}=s-a^{*}a. (51)

Here aa and a∗a^{*} are the creation and annihilation operators, so we have a representation of the angular momentum algebra in the oscillator basis. For large s and appropriate states, this transformation can be reduced to

L+=2​s​a+𝒪⁡(s−12)L−=2​s​a∗+𝒪⁡(s−12)L3=s−n.L_{+}=\sqrt{2s}a+{\mathcal{O}}(s^{-\frac{1}{2}})\quad L_{-}=\sqrt{2s}a^{*}+{\mathcal{O}}(s^{-\frac{1}{2}})\quad L_{3}=s-n. (52)

Notice that in the Holstein Primakoff basis, the spin coherent state |s⟩|s\rangle is transformed to the ground state |0⟩H​P|0\rangle_{HP}, hence the state |n⟩H​P|n\rangle_{HP} corresponds to |s−n⟩|s-n\rangle in the standard angular momentum L3L_{3} eigenbasis. We arrive at

H​(s,𝐰)H​P=(w1​(X−ξ)2+w2​(P−η)2+w3s​(s−a∗​a−ζ)2)+𝒪⁡(s−12).H(s,\mathbf{w})_{HP}=\Big(w_{1}(X-\xi)^{2}+w_{2}(P-\eta)^{2}+\frac{w_{3}}{s}(s-a^{*}a-\zeta)^{2}\Big)\;+{\mathcal{O}}(s^{-\frac{1}{2}}). (53)

Here ξ,η\xi,\eta and ζ\zeta denote the transformed expectation values. From II.1 we know that |s⟩|s\rangle has minimal uncertainty for w∼(1,1,1)w\sim(1,1,1) and arbitrary ss. Based on this observation we make the assumption that we are close to the L3L_{3} spin coherent state. We thus have s≫⟨a∗​a⟩s\gg\langle a^{*}a\rangle and λ3≈s\lambda_{3}\approx s, hence ζ\zeta is linear in ss. Furthermore we can order the weights, such that w1≤w2≤w3w_{1}\leq w_{2}\leq w_{3} to minimize the expectation value. Now we take the limit and let ss becomes large, the operator converges to harmonic oscillator

H​(𝐰)H​P=w1​X2+w2​P2.H(\mathbf{w})_{HP}=w_{1}X^{2}+w_{2}P^{2}. (54)

Here we use that the expectation value of the harmonic oscillator is translation-invariant in phase space, so that we can choose ξ\xi and η\eta to be zero. The state which minimizes the expectation of this operator is simply the harmonic oscillator ground state ψ⁡(m,ω)\psi(m,\omega), with m=12​w2m=\frac{1}{2w_{2}} and ω=4​w1​w2\omega=\sqrt{4w_{1}w_{2}}. In the following these will be combined in the parameter α:=m​ω=w1w2\alpha:=m\omega=\sqrt{\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}}. For the comparison of this result with numerical calculations using the above described algorithm, we must express these ground states in a common basis |n⟩H​P|n\rangle_{HP}, i.e. decomposing ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) in the basis of a harmonic oscillator with α=1\alpha=1. This transformation is given by

ψn:=⟨n|ψ⁡(α)⟩=(α)142n​π​n!​∫Hn​(x)​exp⁡(−(1+α)2​x2)​𝑑x,\psi_{n}:=\langle n|\psi(\alpha)\rangle=\frac{(\alpha)^{\frac{1}{4}}}{\sqrt{2^{n}\pi n!}}\int H_{n}(x)\exp\left(-\frac{(1+\alpha)}{2}x^{2}\right)dx, (55)

which is zero for odd nn and can be solved for even nn through

∫Hn​(x)​exp⁡(−c​x2)​𝑑x=i3​n​π​n!​(c−1)n2n2!​cn+12.\int H_{n}(x)\exp(-cx^{2})dx=\frac{i^{3n}\sqrt{\pi}n!(c-1)^{\frac{n}{2}}}{\frac{n}{2}!c^{\frac{n+1}{2}}}. (56)

The corresponding probability distribution is given by

pn:=|ψn|2=α1+α​(1−α)n(2+2​α)n​n!(n2!)2​(1+(−1)n).p_{n}:=|\psi_{n}|^{2}=\frac{\sqrt{\alpha}}{1+\alpha}\frac{(1-\alpha)^{n}}{(2+2\alpha)^{n}}\frac{n!}{(\frac{n}{2}!)^{2}}(1+(-1)^{n}). (57)

Because this is zero for odd nn, we can set n=2​kn=2k and get

p2​k=2​α1+α​(1−α)2​k(2+2​α)2​k​(2​kk).p_{2k}=\frac{2\sqrt{\alpha}}{1+\alpha}\frac{(1-\alpha)^{2k}}{(2+2\alpha)^{2k}}\binom{2k}{k}. (58)

The above approximation does not necessarily yield the optimal states and it is not rigorously justified so far. As a first step, we compare the distribution pnp_{n} with numerically determined ones for finite ss. These tend to converge as shown in FIG. 8.

Theorem 4.

The lower bound of the asymptotic uncertainty region on a scale of 1/ss is fully described by the generalized Robertson inequality (49) and is saturated by the states ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha).

Proof.

First we will show that the approximation (52) is justified for ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) and evaluate the corresponding asymptotic variances. While the generalized Robertson inequality gets stronger for increasing ss, every extremal point of the corresponding boundary is attained by ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha), which will prove the above statement. Moreover, by truncating the sequence ψn​(α)\psi_{n}(\alpha) at n=2​s+1n=2s+1 and renormalizing, we get a sequence of spin-ss states well approximating ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) as ss goes to infinity.
With this in mind, we will prove the above statement in two steps:
(i) On the one hand we have to verify that lims→∞1s​L+​|ψ⁡(α)⟩=2​a​|ψ⁡(α)⟩\lim\limits_{s\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}L_{+}|\psi(\alpha)\rangle=\sqrt{2}a|\psi(\alpha)\rangle and lims→∞1s​L−​|ψ⁡(α)⟩=2​a∗​|ψ⁡(α)⟩\lim\limits_{s\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}L_{-}|\psi(\alpha)\rangle=\sqrt{2}a^{*}|\psi(\alpha)\rangle which is true if ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) is in the domain of a∗​aa^{*}a. On the other hand we have to show that the term w3s​(s−a∗​a−ζ)2\frac{w_{3}}{s}(s-a^{*}a-\zeta)^{2} from (53) will vanish for ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) with ζ=⟨ψ⁡(α)|s−a∗​a|ψ⁡(α)⟩\zeta=\langle\psi(\alpha)|s-a^{*}a|\psi(\alpha)\rangle as ss goes to infinity. In the Holstein-Primakoff occupation basis |n⟩H​P|n\rangle_{HP}, these moments are given by series of the form

∑n=0∞nc​pn=∑k=0∞(2​k)c​p2​k,\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}n^{c}p_{n}=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\infty}(2k)^{c}p_{2k}, (59)

and can be computed as derivatives using the generating function

c11−4​x=c1​∑n=0∞xk​(2​kk)\frac{c_{1}}{\sqrt{1-4x}}=c_{1}\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}x^{k}\binom{2k}{k} (60)

of the probability distribution p2​kp_{2k} (58). By straightforward calculations we get

⟨ψ⁡(α)|a∗​a|ψ⁡(α)⟩\displaystyle\langle\psi(\alpha)|a^{*}a|\psi(\alpha)\rangle =(1−α)24​α\displaystyle=\frac{(1-\alpha)^{2}}{4\alpha} (61)
⟨ψ⁡(α)|(a∗​a)2|ψ⁡(α)⟩\displaystyle\langle\psi(\alpha)|(a^{*}a)^{2}|\psi(\alpha)\rangle =3​(1−α)416​α2+(1−α)22​α,\displaystyle=\frac{3(1-\alpha)^{4}}{16\alpha^{2}}+\frac{(1-\alpha)^{2}}{2\alpha}, (62)

which is finite for α>0\alpha>0.
(ii) Now the asymptotic variances for ψ⁡(a)\psi(a) can be determined. For ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) the operators 1s​L1\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}L_{1}, 1s​L2\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}L_{2} and 1s​L3\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}L_{3} converge to PP, QQ and a multiple of the identity, we obtain

lims→∞1s​Δψ⁡(α)2​(L1)\displaystyle\lim\limits_{s\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{s}\Delta^{2}_{\psi(\alpha)}(L_{1}) =Δψ⁡(α)2​(Q)=12​α\displaystyle=\Delta^{2}_{\psi(\alpha)}(Q)=\frac{1}{2\alpha} (63)
lims→∞1s​Δψ⁡(α)2​(L2)\displaystyle\lim\limits_{s\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{s}\Delta^{2}_{\psi(\alpha)}(L_{2}) =Δψ⁡(α)2​(P)=α2\displaystyle=\Delta^{2}_{\psi(\alpha)}(P)=\frac{\alpha}{2} (64)
lims→∞1s​Δψ⁡(α)2​(L3)\displaystyle\lim\limits_{s\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{s}\Delta^{2}_{\psi(\alpha)}(L_{3}) =lims→∞1s​Δψ⁡(α)2​(s−a∗​a)=0.\displaystyle=\lim\limits_{s\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{s}\Delta^{2}_{\psi(\alpha)}(s-a^{*}a)=0. (65)

This set of variance triples (12​α,α2,0)(\frac{1}{2\alpha},\frac{\alpha}{2},0) saturates the asymptotic generalized Robertson bound (49). Moreover they describe the extremal boundary curves, see the proof of theorem 2, of the associated uncertainty region. ∎

III Preparation uncertainty: Special topics

III.1 The vector model and moment problems

This may be a good place to comment on the so-called vector model of angular momentum, as it was suggested by Old Quantum Theory. It still seems to be quite popular in teaching, although theoreticians tend to deride it as ridiculously classical and obviously inconsistent. Indeed, its two-particle version gives manifestly false predictions even for spin-1/2, as witnessed by Bell’s (CHSH) inequality. Since any local classical model fails this test, not much can be learned about angular momentum from this observation. Therefore we consider here only the one-particle version, and try to sort out how far it can be trusted.

The basic rationale of the vector model is shown in FIG. 9: Angular momentum is thought of as a classical random variable taking values on a sphere of radius rs=s⁡(s+1)r_{s}=\sqrt{s(s+1)}. For an eigenstate |m⟩|m\rangle the corresponding classical distribution is supposed to be concentrated at latitude mm, and uniform with respect to rotations around the 3-axis. The expectation value of this distribution is (0,0,m)(0,0,m). Moreover, its matrix of second moments is also diagonal, since the coordinate axes are clearly the inertial axes of a mass uniformly distributed on a circle of fixed latitude. One readily checks that all second moments are the same as for the corresponding quantum state. This can be generalized:

Proposition 5.

For any quantum state ρ\rho on ℋ{\mathcal{H}} there is a classical probability distribution μ\mu on the sphere of radius s⁡(s+1)\sqrt{s(s+1)} which has the same first and second moments as the angular momentum in ρ\rho, i.e.,

mj=∫μ⁡(𝑑x)​xj=trρ​LjandMj​k=∫μ⁡(𝑑x)​xj​xk=ℜ⁡e​trρ​Lj​Lk.m_{j}=\int\mu(dx)\,x_{j}=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho L_{j}\qquad\mbox{and}\quad M_{jk}=\int\mu(dx)\,x_{j}x_{k}=\Re e\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho L_{j}L_{k}. (66)

For the proof we only need a characterization of the moments (mj,Mj​k)(m_{j},M_{jk}) of probability measures on a sphere of radius rr, which turns out to be quite simple. This in turn provides an immediate proof of Proposition 5, since the quantum moments Mj​k=ℜ⁡e​trρ​Lj​LkM_{jk}=\Re e\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho L_{j}L_{k}, mj=trρ​Ljm_{j}=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho L_{j} obviously have the required properties with radius r2=s⁡(s+1)r^{2}=s(s+1).

Lemma 6.

Let (mj)∈ℝ(m_{j})\in{\mathbb{R}} for j=1,2,3j=1,2,3, and (Mj​k)j,k=13(M_{jk})_{j,k=1}^{3} a real symmetric 3×33\times 3-matrix. Then these numbers are the first and second moments of a probability distribution on the sphere of radius rr if and only if trM=r2\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits M=r^{2} and the covariance matrix Mj​k−mj​mkM_{jk}-m_{j}m_{k} is positive semi-definite.

Proof.

Necessity is obvious because covariance matrices are always positive and the function v↦∑jvj2=r2v\mapsto\sum_{j}v_{j}^{2}=r^{2} is constant on the sphere. For the converse consider the set KK of moments (m,M)(m,M) of probability measures on the sphere. This is a compact convex set, which we can think of as embedded into 3+6−13+6-1 dimensional real space, because the real symmetric matrix MM is specified by 66 parameters, and we have an additional linear constraint trM=r2\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits M=r^{2}. By the separation theorems for compact convex sets the set KK is therefore completely characterized by a collection of affine inequalities

f⁡(m,M)=trA​M−b⋅m+γ≥0,f(m,M)=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits AM-b\cdot m+\gamma\geq 0, (67)

where AA is real symmetric, b∈ℝ3b\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} with the dot indicating scalar product, and γ∈ℝ\gamma\in{\mathbb{R}}. The functionals for which these inequalities have to be satisfied are precisely those for which the above inequality holds for all pure probability measures, i.e., for Mj​k=vj​vkM_{jk}=v_{j}v_{k} mj=vjm_{j}=v_{j} for some v∈ℝ3v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} on the sphere. In this case we slightly abuse notation and write f⁡(m,M)=f⁡(v)f(m,M)=f(v).

Not all inequalities are needed to characterize KK, but only the extremal ones, which furnish a minimal subset from which all the others follow as linear combinations with positive scalar factors. In particular, we can assume that ff is not strictly positive, so has a zero f⁡(u)=0f(u)=0, which then also has to be a minimum. The extremality condition gives 2​A​u−b=2​λ​u2Au-b=2\lambda u, where λ∈ℝ\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}} is a Lagrange multiplier. This determines bb, and from f⁡(u)=0f(u)=0 we get γ\gamma, so that we can rewrite

f⁡(v)=(v−u)⋅A⁡(v−u)+2​λ​u⋅(v−u).f(v)=(v-u)\cdot A(v-u)+2\lambda u\cdot(v-u). (68)

Now since u,vu,v lie on a sphere of radius rr, we can write 2​u⋅(v−u)=−(v−u)2+(v2−u2)=−(v−u)22u\cdot(v-u)=-(v-u)^{2}+(v^{2}-u^{2})=-(v-u)^{2}, so we can combine the two terms, and obtain again the form (68), with AA modified by a multiple of the identity, and λ=0\lambda=0.

It remains to determine all real symmetric matrices AA such that (v−u)⋅A⁡(v−u)≥0(v-u)\cdot A(v-u)\geq 0, whenever u,vu,v lie on a sphere of radius rr. Equivalently, ξ⋅A​ξ≥0\xi\cdot A\xi\geq 0 for all multiples of vectors of the form v−uv-u. But this set is dense in ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. Hence the desired condition is just the positive semi-definiteness of AA. The resulting inequality for (m,M)(m,M) can be rewritten in terms of the covariance matrix Vj​k=Mj​k−mj​mkV_{jk}=M_{jk}-m_{j}m_{k} as

f⁡(m,M)=trV​A+(m−u)⋅A⁡(m−u)≥0.f(m,M)=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits VA+(m-u)\cdot A(m-u)\geq 0. (69)

Since the second term is anyhow positive, the positive semidefiniteness of VV is sufficient for all these inequalities. This shows the sufficiency of the conditions stated in the Lemma. ∎

Let us make some remarks, which all fit into a fruitful analogy here with the phase space case, i.e., the case of two canonical operators P,QP,Q, and moment problems posed in the respective contexts.

  1. 1.

    The phase space analogue of Prop. 5 is the statement that for any quantum state the first and second moments can also be realized by a classical probability distribution on phase space. Of course, not all classically allowed first and second moments can arise in this way: This is just the theme of preparation uncertainty relations.

  2. 2.

    The classical probability measure μ\mu is not uniquely defined by ρ\rho. For example, the density operator ρ=(2​s+1)−1​1​I\rho=(2s+1)^{-1}{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI} can either be represented by the uniform distribution on the sphere, or by an equal-weight mixture of the distributions with constant latitude mm (in any direction). In the phase space case it is well-known that with the given, quantum-realizable moments one can always find a Gaussian state, which is defined as the distribution with the maximal entropy given those moments. The same idea also works for angular momentum, and it gives probability densities which are the exponential of a quadratic form in the variables. In contrast to the phase space case, when approaching eigenstates (any direction, any mm) this entropy will go to −∞-\infty, since for eigenstates only the singular measures depicted in FIG. 9 can be used.

  3. 3.

    Prop. 5 is certainly false if we include higher than second moments. For example, consider a pure qubit state with m=+1/2m=+1/2. Without loss of generality we can choose the measure μ\mu invariant under rotations around the 3-axis. Since μ\mu must be concentrated on m=1/2m=1/2, this uniquely fixes the measure μ\mu, and hence the moments to all orders. Now consider a direction 𝐞{\mathbf{e}} which is at an angle strictly between 00 and π/2\pi/2 to 𝐞3{\mathbf{e}}_{3}. Then the quantum expectation of (𝐞⋅𝐋)3=𝐞⋅𝐋/4({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}})^{3}={{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}/4 is (𝐞⋅𝐞3)/8({\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{e}}_{3})/8, but the classical expectation of (x⋅𝐞)3(x{\cdot}{\mathbf{e}})^{3} is larger, reflecting the non-linearity of the cube function.

  4. 4.

    The quantum analogue of the classical Hamburger moment would be to reconstruct a quantum state from the set of moments, i.e., the expectations of the monomials in the basic operators (P,QP,Q, or L1,L2,L3L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}). Commutation relations impose some constraints on these moments, so that in the end only monomials like L1n1​L2n2​L3n3L_{1}^{n_{1}}L_{2}^{n_{2}}L_{3}^{n_{3}} need to be considered. Of course, the expectation values of such operators will generally be complex numbers. Can we do the reconstruction for arbitrary states in the spin-ss representation? Indeed, we can, and it is actually much easier than in the phase space case since only finitely many moments suffice. The basic observation is that the moments fix all expectations on the von Neumann algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} generated by the LiL_{i}. Because the representation is irreducible, the commutant of this algebra consists of the multiples of the identity. Hence 𝒜\mathcal{A} must be the full matrix algebra, and the state is uniquely determined. That finitely moments suffice is clear because dim𝒜<∞\dim\mathcal{A}<\infty.

  5. 5.

    Noncommutative moment problems are plagued by “operator ordering” issues. But in some sense we have already adopted a standard “symmetrized” solution for operator ordering, namely to form moments only of the operators 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}} for all fixed 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}. This is analogous in the phase space case to considering the moments of linear combinations of PP and QQ. Now, famously, the full distributions of all such combinations are correctly rendered by the Wigner distribution function, which is itself hardly ever positive [16]. The analogy to the angular momentum case is immediate. So what do we get if we accept “quasi-probability distributions”? Can every state be represented like that? This is answered by the following proposition.

Proposition 7.

Let ρ\rho be a quantum state in the spin-ss representation. Then there is a unique tempered distribution 𝒲ρ{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho} on ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, which is formally real, has support in a ball of radius ss and satisfies, for all 𝐞{\mathbf{e}} and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}

∫d​𝜼​𝒲ρ​(𝜼)​(𝐞⋅𝜼)n=tr(ρ​(𝐞⋅𝐋)n).\int d{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\ {\mathcal{W}}_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\eta}})\,({\mathbf{e}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\eta}})^{n}=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\bigl(\rho({{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}})^{n}\bigr)\ . (70)
Proof.

We can compute the Fourier transform of 𝒲ρ{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho} directly from (70), by multiplying with (i​k)n/n!(ik)^{n}/n! and summing over nn. This turns the left side into the Fourier integral over 𝒲ρ{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho} allowing the sum to be evaluated also on the right hand side:

𝒲^ρ​(𝐤)=∫d​𝜼​𝒲ρ​(𝜼)​ei​𝐤⋅𝜼=tr(ρ​ei​𝐤⋅𝐋),\widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho}({\mathbf{k}})=\int d{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\ {\mathcal{W}}_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\eta}})\,e^{i{\mathbf{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\eta}}}=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\Bigl(\rho e^{i{\mathbf{k}}\cdot{\mathbf{L}}}\Bigr), (71)

where 𝐤=k​𝐞{\mathbf{k}}=k{\mathbf{e}}. Strictly speaking this computation should be regularized by multiplying with an arbitrary test function before summation, but this would lead to the same explicit representation of the Fourier transform 𝒲^ρ\widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho} as a bounded 𝒞∞{\mathcal{C}}^{\infty}-function. This shows that the desired tempered distribution 𝒲ρ{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho} is essentially unique, and can be defined for every ρ\rho. It is formally real, because 𝒲^ρ​(−𝐤)=𝒲^ρ​(𝐤)¯\widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho}(-{\mathbf{k}})=\overline{\widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho}({\mathbf{k}})}. For the claim about the support we invoke the distributional version of the Paley-Wiener-Schwartz Theorem [13, Thm. 7.3.1]. According to that theorem we need to show only that for real vectors 𝐤,κ{\mathbf{k}},{\mathbf{\kappa}} the estimate

|tr(ρ​ei⁡(𝐤+i​κ)⋅𝐋)|≤C​es​|κ|\left|\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\bigl(\rho e^{i({\mathbf{k}}+i{\mathbf{\kappa}})\cdot{\mathbf{L}}}\bigr)\right|\leq Ce^{s|{\mathbf{\kappa}}|} (72)

holds for some constant CC. Treating the sum in the exponential by the Trotter formula, which we may, because these are finite dimensional matrices, we get

‖ei⁡(𝐤+i​κ)⋅𝐋‖=limN→∞‖(ei⁡(𝐤/n)⋅𝐋e(−κ/n)⋅𝐋)n‖≤limN→∞(e(κ/n)​‖𝐋‖)n=es​|κ|.\left\|e^{i({\mathbf{k}}+i{\mathbf{\kappa}})\cdot{\mathbf{L}}}\right\|=\lim_{N\to\infty}\left\|\left(e^{i({\mathbf{k}}/n)\cdot{\mathbf{L}}}\ e^{(-{\mathbf{\kappa}}/n)\cdot{\mathbf{L}}}\right)^{n}\right\|\leq\lim_{N\to\infty}\left(e^{({\mathbf{\kappa}}/n)\|{\mathbf{L}}\|}\right)^{n}=e^{s|{\mathbf{\kappa}}|}. (73)

Clearly this implies the desired estimate. ∎

This Proposition is remarkable in comparison to Prop. 5: If we insist on positivity but require only the first two moments to be correct, the vector model requires a sphere of radius s⁡(s+1)\sqrt{s(s+1)}. On the other hand, if we waive instead the positivity of the classical distribution, we are forced to use a ball of radius ss.

One might ask at this point, in continuation of the above analogies to the phase space case, whether there are “classical” states, for which the Wigner function 𝒲ρ{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho} is a positive function. However, this is easily seen to be impossible. Indeed, when the marginal of a proper probability distribution has support on {−s,…,s}\{-s,\ldots,s\}, the measure itself has to have support on a union of hyperplanes {𝜼|𝜼⋅𝐞=m}\{{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\,|\,{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\cdot{\mathbf{e}}=m\}. But these families of hyperplanes, drawn for various 𝐞{\mathbf{e}} have empty intersection, contradicting the normalization of the measure.

The main use of Wigner functions on phase space is the visualization of quantum states. Unfortunately, the much more singular nature of 𝒲ρ{\mathcal{W}}_{\rho} for angular momentum will prevent these Wigner functions from becoming similarly popular. This irregularity can be tamed by replacing on the right hand side of (71)

ei​𝐤⋅𝐋↦ei​k1​L1​ei​k2​L2​ei​k3​L3.e^{\textstyle i{\mathbf{k}}\cdot{\mathbf{L}}}\mapsto e^{\textstyle ik_{1}L_{1}}\ e^{\textstyle ik_{2}L_{2}}\ e^{\textstyle ik_{3}L_{3}}. (74)

The corresponding distribution is then a sum of point measures sitting on a finite cubical grid [7]. This may actually be useful in quantum information, where it relates to a discrete phase space structure over the cyclic group of d=2​s+1d=2s+1 elements. However, for angular momentum proper we find this breaking of rotational symmetry abhorrent.

III.2 Entropic uncertainty

In this section we will have a look at the entropic uncertainty relations. Given a measurement of a hermitian operator A=∑iai​PiA=\sum_{i}a_{i}P_{i}, with eigenprojectors PiP_{i}, the probability of obtaining the ithi^{\rm th} measurement outcome will be denoted by πi​(ρ)=tr(ρ​Pi)\pi_{i}(\rho)=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits(\rho P_{i}) and the associated probability distribution as π⁡(ρ)={π1​(ρ),⋯,πd​(ρ)}\pi(\rho)=\{\pi_{1}(\rho),\cdots,\pi_{d}(\rho)\}. Then the output entropy of AA in the state ρ\rho is defined as the Shannon entropy of π⁡(ρ)\pi(\rho)

H(A,ρ):=H(π(ρ))=−∑i=1dπi(ρ)logd(πi(ρ)),\displaystyle H(A,\rho):=H(\pi(\rho))=-\sum\limits_{i=1}^{d}\pi_{i}(\rho)\log_{d}(\pi_{i}(\rho)), (75)

which serves as an uncertainty measure. Note that we normalize the Shannon entropy by its maximal value log⁡d\log d so that all occurring entropies are bounded by 11. In contrast to the variance, the entropy of a probability distribution does not change by permuting or rescaling the measurement outcomes and so only depends on the choice of the PiP_{i} (up to permutations) and not on the eigenvalues aia_{i}. This implies that an entropic uncertainty relation, which constrains the output entropies of two (for simplicity non-degenerate) observables A,BA,B, only depends on the unitary operator UU connecting the respective eigenbases. A well-known bound in this setting is the general Maassen-Uffink bound [20]

H⁡(A,ρ)+H⁡(B,ρ)\displaystyle H(A,\rho)+H(B,\rho) ≥\displaystyle\geq −2​logd​(c)\displaystyle-2\log_{d}(c) (76)
c=c⁡(U)\displaystyle c=c(U) =\displaystyle= maxi​j⁡|Ui​j|.\displaystyle\max\limits_{ij}|U_{ij}|. (77)

For angular momentum measurements in two orthogonal directions the connecting unitary operators are rotations, i.e., given as a rotation by π/2\pi/2 around the third coordinate axis according to the spin-ss representation of S​O​(3)SO(3) on ℂ2​s+1{\mathbb{C}}^{2s+1}. For arbitrary angles these representations are called Wigner-D matrices [2] and will also be used in Sect. IV.5. It turns out that the Maassen-Uffink bound is in general not optimal, but describes precisely the uncertainty region for s→∞s\to\infty.

For spin s=1s=1, the uncertainty region can still be reliably investigated by parameterizing the set of pure states in the L3L_{3} eigenbasis. Numerics suggests that real valued states and their permutations characterize the lower bound of the uncertainty region. The resulting uncertainty regions for two and three components are shown in FIG. 10, which should be compared directly to FIG. 4(left) and FIG. 3(right).

The marked lines in FIG. 10 correspond to states of a form |ϕ⁡(t)⟩:=(cos⁡(t)2,sin⁡(t),cos⁡(t)2)|\phi(t)\rangle:=\left(\frac{\cos(t)}{\sqrt{2}},\sin(t),\frac{\cos(t)}{\sqrt{2}}\right), written in L3L_{3}-eigenbasis, and their permutations. They correspond exactly to the extremal curves found for variance uncertainty as shown in FIG. 3. Remarkably, however, the ordering of “uncertainties” turns out to be different in the two cases. Consider the L2L_{2}-eigenstates, which are shown in the left panels of both 2D Figures 4 and 10 as the points on the horizontal axis. The respective L1L_{1}-probability distribution are (1/4,1/2,1/4)(1/4,1/2,1/4) for m=±1m=\pm 1 and (1/2,0,1/2)(1/2,0,1/2) for m=0m=0. The former distribution has the larger entropy ((3/2)​log3​2>log3⁡2(3/2)\log_{3}2>\log_{3}2) but the smaller variance (1/2<11/2<1).

For larger ss this inversion no longer holds. FIG. 11 shows this effect. Because we can exchange the roles of L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} by a unitary rotation, the uncertainty diagrams are symmetric with respect to the diagonal. Therefore the optimal linear bound must be of the form (76), with a suitable cc. The entropy sums for the eigenstates |m⟩|m\rangle with minimal and maximal |m||m| are shown in FIG. 11. For all half-integer ss and for integer s>7s>7 the coherent state |s⟩|s\rangle produces not only the lowest variance, but also the lowest entropy. FIG. 11 also shows the Maassen-Uffink bound, which has been computed by Sánchez-Ruiz [30]. It is attained for the overlap of two spin coherent states and is given by

c2=2−2​s​(2​s[s+1/2]).\displaystyle c^{2}=2^{-2s}\binom{2s}{[s+1/2]}. (78)

s=1s=1 seems to be the only case in which the bound is tight.

However, for large ss, the bound is again optimal, as the following result shows.

Proposition 8.

In the limit s→∞s\rightarrow\infty the optimal lower bound on the entropic uncertainty region of L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} is given by the Maassen-Uffink inequality, which converges to

H⁡(L1,ρ)+H⁡(L2,ρ)≥12.\displaystyle H(L_{1},\rho)+H(L_{2},\rho)\geq\frac{1}{2}. (79)
Proof.

As a first step we will compute the asymptotic behavior of the bound −log2​s+1⁡[c2]-\log_{2s+1}[c^{2}], with cc given in (78). Expanding the central binomial coefficient in factorials and using the Stirling approximation up to order log2​s+1⁡(s)\log_{2s+1}(s) gives

lims→∞−log2​s+1[c2]=lims→∞−log2​s+1[2−2​s(2​s[s+1/2])]=1/2,\displaystyle\lim\limits_{s\to\infty}-\log_{2s+1}[c^{2}]=\lim\limits_{s\to\infty}-\log_{2s+1}\left[2^{-2s}\binom{2s}{[s+1/2]}\right]=1/2, (80)

which proves the convergence of the Maassen-Uffink bound to the right hand side of (79).

In order to show that this bound describes the asymptotic uncertainty region, we have to exhibit sequences of states saturating for every point on the boundary curve. We first show that the endpoint (0,1/2)(0,1/2) is asymptotically attained by the L1L_{1}-eigenstates |s⟩|s\rangle: The output entropy of |s⟩|s\rangle in the L1L_{1} basis is always zero, whereas the output entropy in the L2L_{2} basis can be evaluated as H⁡(L2,|s⟩)=H⁡(L1,U3​|s⟩)H(L_{2},|s\rangle)=H(L_{1},U_{3}|s\rangle), with U3=e−i​π2​L3U_{3}=e^{-\frac{i\pi}{2}L_{3}}. Because |s⟩|s\rangle has maximal quantum number mm, the probability amplitudes of U3​|s⟩U_{3}|s\rangle are given by the last column of the Wigner-D Matrix U3=D⁡(0,π/2,0)U_{3}=D(0,\pi/2,0). By expanding the Wigner-D matrix in terms of Jacobi polynomials [2], one can verify that πm​(U3​|s⟩)=|⟨m|U3|s⟩|2\pi_{m}(U_{3}|s\rangle)=|{\langle m|}{U_{3}}|s\rangle|^{2} is a binomial distribution in mm, symmetric on the domain {−s,s}\{-s,s\}. The entropy of this distribution is −1/2log2​s+1(2πe2​s+14)+𝒪(1n)-1/2\log_{2s+1}(2\pi e\frac{2s+1}{4})+\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{n}), which converges to 12\frac{1}{2} as ss goes to infinity, hence (79) can be saturated:

lims→∞(H⁡(L1,|s⟩),H⁡(L2,|s⟩))=(0,12).\displaystyle\lim\limits_{s\to\infty}\Bigl(H(L_{1},|s\rangle),H(L_{2},|s\rangle)\Bigr)=\bigl(0,{\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\bigr). (81)

Finally we have to construct states saturating every point of this bound. For |s⟩|s\rangle, still in the eigenbasis of L1L_{1}, and arbitrary ss, we define a family of unit vectors |ψα⟩|\psi_{\alpha}\rangle as

|ψα⟩=cα​(cos⁡(α)​|s⟩+sin⁡(α)​U3​|s⟩).\displaystyle|\psi_{\alpha}\rangle=c_{\alpha}\left(\cos(\alpha)|s\rangle+\sin(\alpha)U_{3}|s\rangle\right). (82)

The L1L_{1}-outcome probability distribution associated with this vector is

πm​(ψα)≈cos⁡(α)2​δm​s+sin⁡(α)2​|⟨m|U3|s⟩|2,\displaystyle\pi_{m}(\psi_{\alpha})\approx\cos(\alpha)^{2}\delta_{ms}+\sin(\alpha)^{2}|{\langle m|}{U_{3}}|s\rangle|^{2}, (83)

because the two probability distributions have practically no overlap for large ss, and hence also cα≈1c_{\alpha}\approx 1. For the same reason we can evaluate the entropy of π⁡(Ψα)\pi(\Psi_{\alpha}) as a sum, obtaining

H⁡(L1,|ψα⟩)\displaystyle H(L_{1},|\psi_{\alpha}\rangle) ≈sin2⁡(α)​H​(L1,U3​|s⟩)+H2​(cos2⁡(α),sin2⁡(α))log2⁡(2​s+1)≈12​sin2⁡(α),\displaystyle\approx\sin^{2}(\alpha)H(L_{1},U_{3}|s\rangle)+\frac{H_{2}(\cos^{2}(\alpha),\sin^{2}(\alpha))}{\log_{2}(2s+1)}\approx\frac{1}{2}\sin^{2}(\alpha), (84)

where H2H_{2} is the binary entropy function. In the L2L_{2}-basis the roles of the two terms in ψα\psi_{\alpha} are exchanged, and we get

H⁡(L2,|ψα⟩)≈12​cos2⁡(α).\displaystyle H(L_{2},|\psi_{\alpha}\rangle)\approx\frac{1}{2}\cos^{2}(\alpha). (85)

Hence the sequence ψα\psi_{\alpha} realizes the point 12​(sin2⁡(α),cos2⁡(α))\frac{1}{2}(\sin^{2}(\alpha),\cos^{2}(\alpha)) on the boundary. ∎

IV Measurement uncertainty

IV.1 Introduction

As mentioned in the introduction, a measurement uncertainty relation is a quantitative bound on the accuracy with which two observables can be measured approximately on the same device. Already in Kennard’s 1927 paper [18] it is clearly stated that in quantum mechanics the notion of a “true value” loses its meaning, so that we should not think of “measurement error” as the deviation of the observed value from a true value. What we can always do, however, is to compare the performance of two measuring devices, one of which is an (perhaps hypothetical) “ideal” measurement and the other an approximate one. The only requirement is that these two measurements give outputs which lie in the same space XX and whose distance is somehow defined. A good approximate measurement is then one which will give, on every input state, almost the same output distribution as the ideal one. This operational focus on the output distributions is also in keeping with the way one would detect a disturbance of the system. Consider how we discover that trying to detect through which of two slits the particles pass disturbs them: The interference pattern, i.e., the output distribution of the interferometer is changed and fringes washed out.

Two related ways to build up a quantitative comparison of distributions, and thereby a quantitative approximation measure between observables, were introduced in the papers [3, 5] and applied to the standard situation of a position and a momentum operator. These two notions, called calibration error and metric error will be described in the following subsections. Either way we get a natural figure of merit for an observable FF jointly measuring two or more components of angular momentum. In fact, we will only treat the case where FF jointly measures all components. By this we simply mean an observable whose output is not a single number but a vector 𝜼{\boldsymbol{\eta}}. From this, one derives a “marginal measurement” F𝐞F^{\mathbf{e}} of the 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}-component by post-processing, i.e., by taking the 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}-component 𝐞⋅𝜼{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\boldsymbol{\eta}} of the output vector as the output of F𝐞F^{\mathbf{e}}. These marginals can then be compared with the standard projection valued measurement of the angular momentum component 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}. When D⁡(G,E)D(G,E) is the quantity chosen to characterize the error of an observable GG with respect to the ideal reference EE we get, in our special case,

Dmax​(F)=max𝐞⁡D⁡(F𝐞,𝐞⋅𝐋)D_{\rm max}(F)=\max_{\mathbf{e}}D(F^{\mathbf{e}},{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}) (86)

is the desired figure of merit. This is the quantity which we will minimize. But first we have to be more explicit about the two choices for the error quantity D⁡(G,E)D(G,E). This will be done in the next two subsections.

IV.2 Calibration Error

The simpler one assumes that the “ideal” observable is projection valued, so that we can produce states which have a very narrow distribution around one of its eigenvalues (or points in the continuous spectrum). In other words, we have some states available which come close to having a “true value” in the sense that the ideal distribution is sharp around a known value. A good approximate measurement should then have an output distribution, which is also well peaked around this value. Thus we only have to compare probability distributions to δ\delta-function like distributions, i.e., point measures δx\delta_{x} with x∈Xx\in X. This is straightforward, and we set, for any probability measure μ\mu on the space XX, 1≤α<∞1\leq\alpha<\infty

Dα​(μ,δx)=(∫Xμ⁡(𝑑y)​D​(y,x)α)1/α,D_{\alpha}(\mu,\delta_{x})=\left(\int_{X}\mu(dy)\ D(y,x)^{\alpha}\right)^{1/\alpha}, (87)

where DD under the integral is the given metric on XX. This could be called the power-α\alpha deviation of μ\mu from the point xx. We are mostly interested in quadratic deviations, i.e., α=2\alpha=2. However, in this section we keep α\alpha general, which causes no extra difficulty, but makes clear which numbers “22” arise directly from the role of the averaging power α\alpha in (87) and similar equations.

We apply this now to FρF_{\rho} the output distribution FρF_{\rho} obtained by measuring the observable FF on the input state ρ\rho, and its ideal counterpart EρE_{\rho}. The ε\varepsilon-deviation or ε\varepsilon-calibration error of the observable FF with respect to the ideal observable EE is

Δαε​(F,E)=sup{Dα​(Fρ,δx)|Dα​(Eρ,δx)≤ε},\Delta_{\alpha}^{\varepsilon}(F,E)=\sup\left\{D_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},\delta_{x})|D_{\alpha}(E_{\rho},\delta_{x})\leq\varepsilon\right\}, (88)

where the supremum is over all x∈Xx\in X and “calibration states” ρ\rho, which are sharply concentrated on xx up to quality ε\varepsilon. Note that as a function of ε\varepsilon this expression is decreasing as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, because the supremum is taken over smaller and smaller sets. Therefore the limit exists, and we define the calibration error of FF with respect to EE by

Δαc​(F,E)=limε→0Δαε​(F,E).\Delta_{\alpha}^{c}(F,E)=\lim\limits_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\Delta_{\alpha}^{\varepsilon}(F,E). (89)

For observables EE with discrete spectrum (like angular momentum components) we can also take ε=0\varepsilon=0, in (88), and directly get Δαc​(F,E)=Δα0​(F,E)\Delta_{\alpha}^{c}(F,E)=\Delta_{\alpha}^{0}(F,E).

IV.3 Metric error

A possible issue with the calibration error is that it describes the performance of FF only on a very special subclass of states. On the one hand this makes it easier to determine it experimentally, but on the other hand we get no guarantee about the performance of the device on general inputs. Classically this problem does not arise, because broad distributions can be represented as mixtures of sharply peaked ones, and this allows us to give an estimate also on the similarity of output distributions for general inputs. The form of this estimate gives a good hint towards how to define the distance of probability distributions both of which are diffuse. Indeed suppose ρ\rho is an input state such that ρ=∫μ⁡(𝑑x)​ρx\rho=\int\mu(dx)\,\rho_{x}, where ρx\rho_{x} is an ε\varepsilon-calibration state at point xx, and μ\mu is an arbitrary probability measure. Then we can define measure γ\gamma on X×XX\times X by γ⁡(d​x​d​y)=μ⁡(d​x)​Fρx​(d​y)\gamma(dx\,dy)=\mu(dx)F_{\rho_{x}}(dy), which gives the probability of the joint event of having a “true value” x∈d​xx\in dx and finding y∈d​yy\in dy. If one integrates out the xx variable one gets the output distribution for ρ\rho, because FρF_{\rho} is linear in ρ\rho, and if one integrates out yy one gets μ\mu, because each FρxF_{\rho_{x}} is normalized. To within ε\varepsilon this is the output distribution EρE_{\rho}, and with known calibration error we get the bound

∫γ⁡(d​x​𝑑y)​D​(x,y)α=∫μ⁡(𝑑x)​∫Fρx​(𝑑y)​D​(x,y)α=∫μ⁡(𝑑x)​Dα​(Fρx,δx)α≤Δαε​(F,E)α.\int\gamma(dx\,dy)\ D(x,y)^{\alpha}=\int\mu(dx)\int F_{\rho_{x}}(dy)\ D(x,y)^{\alpha}=\int\mu(dx)D_{\alpha}(F_{\rho_{x}},\delta_{x})^{\alpha}\leq\Delta_{\alpha}^{\varepsilon}(F,E)^{\alpha}. (90)

This suggests the following definitions. For two probability distributions μ\mu and ν\nu on XX we define a coupling to be a measure γ\gamma on X×XX\times X whose first marginal is μ\mu and whose second marginal is ν\nu. The set of couplings will be denoted by Γ⁡(μ,ν)\Gamma(\mu,\nu), and is always non-empty because it contains the product measure. We then define the Wasserstein α\alpha-distance of μ\mu and ν\nu as

Dα​(μ,ν)=infγ∈Γ⁡(μ,ν)(∫γ⁡(d​x​𝑑y)​D​(x,y)α)1/α.D_{\alpha}(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)}\left(\int\gamma(dx\,dy)\ D(x,y)^{\alpha}\right)^{1/\alpha}. (91)

This is also called a transport distance, because of the following interpretation, first seen by Gaspar Monge in the 18th century who considered the building of fortifications. We consider μ\mu and ν\nu as some distribution of earth, and the task of a builder who wants to transform distribution μ\mu into distribution ν\nu. The workers are paid by the bucket and the power α\alpha of the distance travelled with each bucket (giving a bonus pay on long distances). The builder’s plan is precisely the coupling γ\gamma saying how many units are to be taken from xx to yy, and the integral is the total cost. The infimum is just the price of the optimal transport plan. The theory of such metrics is well developed, and we recommend the book of Villani [32] on the subject, but in the present context we only need some simple observations.

With a metric between probability distributions we define the distance of two observables as the worst case distance of their output distributions:

Dα​(F,E):=supρDα​(Fρ,Eρ).D_{\alpha}(F,E):=\sup_{\rho}D_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},E_{\rho}). (92)

For the connection between this metric error and the calibration error introduced above, note first that when ν\nu is the point measure δx\delta_{x}, and μ\mu is arbitrary the product is the only coupling, and the two definitions Dα​(μ,δx)D_{\alpha}(\mu,\delta_{x}) from equations (87) and (91) coincide. Therefore, if Dα​(Eρ,δx)≤εD_{\alpha}(E_{\rho},\delta_{x})\leq\varepsilon, we have

Dα​(Fρ,δx)≤Dα​(Fρ,Eρ)+Dα​(Eρ,δx)≤Dα​(F,E)+ε.D_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},\delta_{x})\leq D_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},E_{\rho})+D_{\alpha}(E_{\rho},\delta_{x})\leq D_{\alpha}(F,E)+\varepsilon. (93)

By taking the supremum (88) and letting ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, we hence have

Δαc​(F,E)≤Dα​(F,E).\Delta_{\alpha}^{c}(F,E)\leq D_{\alpha}(F,E). (94)

Intuitively, this merely indicates that for calibration we test deviations only in the small subset of highly concentrated states. Then (90) is a partial converse: If ρ\rho has a convex decomposition into ε\varepsilon-concentrated states, Dα​(Fρ,μ)≤Δαε​(F,E)D_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},\mu)\leq\Delta_{\alpha}^{\varepsilon}(F,E), and since Dα​(μ,Eρ)≤εD_{\alpha}(\mu,E_{\rho})\leq\varepsilon we get Dα​(Fρ,Eρ)≤Δαε​(F,E)+εD_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},E_{\rho})\leq\Delta_{\alpha}^{\varepsilon}(F,E)+\varepsilon. In the classical case such a decomposition always exists, so we have equality Dα​(Fρ,Eρ)=Δαc​(F,E)D_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},E_{\rho})=\Delta_{\alpha}^{c}(F,E). In the quantum case, however, we not only have convex mixtures of sharply concentrated states but also coherent superpositions. Using these it is easy to build examples in which (94) is strict.

There is a second “quasi-classical” setting, in which calibration and metric error coincide, and this will actually be used below. This is the case when FF and EE differ only by classical noise generated in the measuring apparatus. More formally this is described by a transition probability kernel P⁡(x,d​y)P(x,dy), which is for every xx the probability measure in yy describing the output of FF, given that EE has been given the value xx. We can think of this as classical probabilistic post-processing or noise. It is, of course, not necessary that FF actually operates in two steps, but only that it could be simulated in this way, i.e., the relation F⁡(𝑑y)=∫E⁡(𝑑x)​P​(x,𝑑y)F(dy)=\int E(dx)\ P(x,dy) holds. This is enough to conclude Δαc​(F,E)=Dα​(F,E)\Delta_{\alpha}^{c}(F,E)=D_{\alpha}(F,E), and to give a formula for both in terms of the size of the noise kernel PP. In the following Lemma the EE-essential supremum of a measurable function ff with respect to a measure EE (denoted E−ess​supx∈X⁡f⁡(x)E\!{\rm-}\!\mathop{\rm ess\,sup}_{x\in X}f(x)) is the supremum of all λ\lambda such that the upper level set {x|f⁡(x)>λ}\{x|f(x)>\lambda\} has non-zero EE-measure. In our application EE is the spectral measure of a component 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}, so it is concentrated on the finite set {−s,…,s}\{-s,\ldots,s\}. The essential supremum is then simply the maximum of ff over this set.

Lemma 9.

Let EE be a projection valued observable on a separable metric space (X,D)(X,D). Let FF be an observable arising from EE by post-processing with a transition probability kernel PP. Then, for all α\alpha,

Δαc​(F,E)=Dα​(F,E)=(E−ess​supx∈X⁡∫P⁡(x,𝑑y)​D​(x,y)α)1/α.\Delta_{\alpha}^{c}(F,E)=D_{\alpha}(F,E)=\left(E\!{\rm-}\!\mathop{\rm ess\,sup}_{x\in X}\int P(x,dy)\ D(x,y)^{\alpha}\right)^{1/\alpha}. (95)
Proof.

Let I, II, III be the three terms in this equation. Then I≤\leqII is given by (94). To show II≤\leqIII, note that for any state ρ\rho we get a coupling γ\gamma between FρF_{\rho} and EρE_{\rho} by γ⁡(d​x​d​y)=Eρ​(d​x)​P​(x,d​y)\gamma(dx\,dy)=E_{\rho}(dx)P(x,dy). Hence

Dα​(Fρ,Eρ)α≤∫γ⁡(d​x​𝑑y)​D​(x,y)α=∫Eρ​(𝑑x)​∫P⁡(x,𝑑y)​D​(x,y)α.D_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},E_{\rho})^{\alpha}\leq\int\gamma(dx\,dy)\ D(x,y)^{\alpha}=\int E_{\rho}(dx)\int P(x,dy)\ D(x,y)^{\alpha}.

Then, by definition of the essential supremum, EρE_{\rho} vanishes on X>X_{>} and on X≤X_{\leq} the integrand is bounded by tαt^{\alpha}. Hence Dα​(Fρ,Eρ)α<tαD_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},E_{\rho})^{\alpha}<t^{\alpha}. Taking the supremum over ρ\rho and the αth\alpha^{\rm th} root we get Dα​(F,E)<tD_{\alpha}(F,E)<t for every t>t>III, proving II≤\leqIII.

It remains to show that III≤\leqI. This time we pick a t<E−ess​supx⁡f⁡(x)t<E\!{\rm-}\!\mathop{\rm ess\,sup}_{x}f(x). By definition, this means that E⁡({x|f⁡(x)>t})≠0E\bigl(\{x|f(x)>t\}\bigr)\neq 0. Now let ε>0\varepsilon>0. Then because we have assumed XX to be separable, it is covered by a countable collection of ε\varepsilon-balls Bε​(xi)={y∈X|D⁡(xi,y)≤ε}B_{\varepsilon}(x_{i})=\{y\in X|D(x_{i},y)\leq\varepsilon\}, i=1,2,…i=1,2,\ldots. Hence due to countable additivity of EE

Hence for some z=xiz=x_{i} we have E⁡(Bε​(z)∩{x|f⁡(x)>t})≠0E\bigl(B_{\varepsilon}(z)\cap\{x|f(x)>t\}\bigr)\neq 0.
