where the second function defines a function gg. We interpret these quantities as LαL^{\alpha}-norms with respect to EρE_{\rho}, i.e., m=‖f‖αm=\|f\|_{\alpha} and Dα​(Fρ,δz)=‖g‖αD_{\alpha}(F_{\rho},\delta_{z})=\|g\|_{\alpha}. Then by the triangle inequality

In [5] a special case of this Lemma was used to show Δc=D\Delta^{c}=D for the position and momentum marginals of a covariant phase space measurement. In that case the noise kernel PP is even translation invariant, i.e., the output of the marginal observable can be simulated by just adding some state-independent noise to the output of the ideal position or momentum observable. Such translation invariance makes no sense in the case of angular momentum, since the range of the outputs m∈{−s,…,s}m\in\{-s,\ldots,s\} of the ideal observable is bounded. This is why the above generalization was needed, in which the noise can depend on the ideal output value. The reason for the existence of a post-processing kernel, however, will be the same as in the phase space case: the covariance of the joint measurement. Roughly speaking this makes the marginal corresponding to 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}} invariant under rotations around the 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}-axis, which in an irreducible representation means that it must be a function of 𝐞⋅𝐋{{\mathbf{e}}{\cdot}{\mathbf{L}}}. It is therefore crucial to argue that the optimal joint measurement is covariant, which will be done in the next section.

IV.4 Covariant Observables

Consider a general observable FF with outcome space XX. Suppose some group GG acts on XX, with the action written (g,x)↦g​x(g,x)\mapsto gx as usual. Suppose that the group also acts as a symmetry group of the quantum system. That is, there is a representation g↦Ugg\mapsto U_{g} of GG by operators UgU_{g}, which are unitary or antiunitary, and satisfy the group law (possibly up to a phase factor). The observable FF is then called covariant if Ug∗​F​(S)​Ug=F⁡(g−1​S)U_{g}^{*}F(S)U_{g}=F(g^{-1}S) for all g∈Gg\in G and every measurable set SS. In other words, shifting the input state by UgU_{g} will result in the entire output distribution shifted by gg. For our purposes it will be convenient to express this in terms of an action F↦Tg​FF\mapsto T_{g}F of GG on the the set of observables:

(Tg​F)​(S)=Ug​F​(g−1​S)​Ug∗.(T_{g}F)(S)=U_{g}F(g^{-1}S)U_{g}^{*}. (102)

Then the covariant observables are precisely those for which Tg​F=FT_{g}F=F for all g∈Gg\in G.

For angular momentum the group will be the rotation group with its action on the 3-vectors (X=ℝ3X={\mathbb{R}}^{3}). The representation UU is then up to a factor ±1\pm 1. Alternatively, we can take GG as the covering group SU⁡(2){\rm SU(2)}. Since the covariant observables are exactly the same this choice is completely equivalent.

Covariance is certainly a reasonable condition to impose on a “good” observable, so it would make sense to study uncertainty relations just for these. However, there is no need for such an ad hoc restriction, because the minimum of uncertainty over all observables is anyway attained on a covariant one. The basic reason for this is that our figure of merit (86) does not single out a direction in space, so that it is invariant under the action TgT_{g}. We therefore only have to show that there is no symmetry breaking, i.e., the symmetric variational problem has a symmetric solution. This will be done in the following Lemma.

Lemma 10.

For any observable FF with an outcome set X=ℝ3X={\mathbb{R}}^{3}, and 1≤α<∞1\leq\alpha<\infty let

Then

    both these functionals are invariant under the action TT, and Dmax​(F)αD_{\rm max}(F)^{\alpha} and Δmax​(F)α\Delta_{\rm max}(F)^{\alpha} are convex.

    each of the infima infFDmax​(F)\inf_{F}D_{\rm max}(F) and infFΔmax​(F)\inf_{F}\Delta_{\rm max}(F) is independent of whether it is taken over all observables or just the covariant ones.

Given any observable FF we now form its average F¯=∫d​R​TR​F\overline{F}=\int dR\ T_{R}F with respect to the normalized Haar measure d​RdR. Then F¯\overline{F} is covariant and Dmax​(F¯)≤∫d​R​Dmax​(TR​F)=Dmax​(F)D_{\rm max}(\overline{F})\leq\int dR\ D_{\rm max}(T_{R}F)=D_{\rm max}(F). infFDmax​(F)≤infF​covariantDmax​(F)≤infFDmax​(F),\inf_{F}D_{\rm max}(F)\leq\inf_{F\ {\rm covariant}}D_{\rm max}(F)\leq\inf_{F}D_{\rm max}(F), (108)

while the first follows trivially because the covariant observables are a subset. Hence the two infima are the same, and the same argument also applies to Δmax\Delta_{\rm max}, proving the second claim. ∎

We could have included also a statement that the infima in this Lemma are all attained. The argument for that is the compactness of the set of observables (in a suitable topology) and the lower semi-continuity of DmaxD_{\rm max} and Δmax\Delta_{\rm max} which follows, like convexity, from the representation of these functionals as the pointwise supremum of continuous functionals. However, since we will later anyhow explicitly exhibit minimizers, we will skip the abstract arguments. We also remark that one of the main difficulties in the position/momentum case [5] does not arise here: In contrast to the group of phase space translations, the rotation group is compact, so the average is an integral and not an “invariant mean”, which has the potential of producing singular measures with some support on infinitely far away points.

The main importance of this Lemma is to make the variational problem much more tractable. For covariant observables we have a fairly explicit parameterization, which allows us to explicitly compute the minimizers. In contrast, for the seemingly easier case of joint measurement of just two components covariance gives only a very weak constraint, and we were not able to complete the minimization.

To develop the form of covariant observables, let us first consider the case when the output vectors have a fixed length rr. A plausible value would be r=sr=s, but we will leave this open. In this case XX reduces to a sphere of radius rr, which is a homogeneous space for the rotation group. We could thus apply the covariant version[29, 33] of the Naimark [22] dilation theorem to obtain a complete classification. But we do not need this machinery in this elementary case. Note first, that trF⁡(d​x)\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits F(dx) is an invariant measure on the sphere, and all probability densities trρ​F​(d​x)\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits\rho F(dx) are bounded by this measure (since ρ\rho is bounded). Hence, for every ρ\rho there is a bounded probability density with respective to the uniform measure. Since this depends linearly on ρ\rho, it is given by a bounded operator depending on 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}. The 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}-dependence is then completely resolved by covariance, and it is sufficient to know this density at one point, say the north pole r​𝝂r{\boldsymbol{\nu}}. Moreover, by covariance this density must commute with the rotations around 𝝂{\boldsymbol{\nu}}, and is hence a linear combination of the eigenstates |n⟩​⟨n|{|n\rangle\langle n|} with n∈{−s,…,s}n\in\{-s,\ldots,s\}. The only choices to be made are hence the coefficients FnF_{n} of this liner combination. We write the resulting observable in terms of its integrals with an arbitrary function hh on the sphere:

∫F⁡(𝑑𝐱)​h​(𝐱)\displaystyle\int F(d{\mathbf{x}})h({\mathbf{x}}) =\displaystyle= (2​s+1)​∫d​R​UR​(∑nFn​|n⟩​⟨n|)​UR∗​h​(r​R​𝝂)\displaystyle(2s+1)\int dR\ U_{R}\Bigl(\sum_{n}F_{n}{|n\rangle\langle n|}\Bigr)U_{R}^{*}\ h(r\,R{\boldsymbol{\nu}}) (109)
=\displaystyle= (2​s+1)​∫sin⁡θ​d​θ​d​ϕ4​π​∑nFn​Uθ,ϕ​|n⟩​⟨n|​Uθ,ϕ∗​h​(r​𝐞θ,ϕ)\displaystyle(2s+1)\int\frac{\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi}{4\pi}\sum_{n}F_{n}U_{\theta,\phi}{|n\rangle\langle n|}U_{\theta,\phi}^{*}\ h(r\,{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta,\phi})

Here the first integral is over Haar measure on the rotation group (or SU⁡(2){\rm SU(2)}), whereas the second is expressed in polar coordinates (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) on the sphere, with 𝐞θ,ϕ{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta,\phi} the corresponding unit vector, and Uθ,ϕU_{\theta,\phi} some rotation rotating the north pole 𝝂{\boldsymbol{\nu}} to 𝐞θ,ϕ{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta,\phi}. It does not matter which rotation we choose, because |n⟩​⟨n|{|n\rangle\langle n|} is invariant with respect to rotations around the 3-axis. The two expressions are related by introducing Euler angles on the rotation group and integrating out the initial rotation around the 3-axis. The normalization factor (2​s+1)(2s+1) is chosen so that the constraints on FnF_{n} are exactly Fn≥0F_{n}\geq 0 and ∑nFn=1\sum_{n}F_{n}=1, i.e., the observable is represented as a convex combination of observables using only one fixed |n⟩​⟨n|{|n\rangle\langle n|} as the density. What changes when rr is not fixed is simply that we get an additional integration over rr, where the FnF_{n} may also depend on rr. Effectively, we get a probability measure Fn​(d​r)F_{n}(dr) on {−s,…,s}×ℝ+\{-s,\ldots,s\}\times{\mathbb{R}}_{+} and the second version of (109) just becomes

∫F⁡(𝑑𝐱)​h​(𝐱)=∑n∫Fn​(𝑑r)​(2​s+1)​∫sin⁡θ​d​θ​d​ϕ4​π​Uθ,ϕ​|n⟩​⟨n|​Uθ,ϕ∗​h​(r​𝐞θ,ϕ).\int F(d{\mathbf{x}})h({\mathbf{x}})=\sum_{n}\int F_{n}(dr)\ (2s+1)\int\frac{\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi}{4\pi}U_{\theta,\phi}{|n\rangle\langle n|}U_{\theta,\phi}^{*}\ h(r\,{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta,\phi}). (110)

The criterion for joint measurability does not depend on the full observable, but only on the marginals along the various directions 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}. It is one of the direct consequences of covariance, evident from the proof of Lemma 10, that Dα​(F𝐞,E𝐞)D_{\alpha}(F^{\mathbf{e}},E^{\mathbf{e}}) and Δαc​(F𝐞,E𝐞)\Delta^{c}_{\alpha}(F^{\mathbf{e}},E^{\mathbf{e}}) do not depend on 𝐞{\mathbf{e}}. We will therefore only consider the case 𝐞=𝝂{\mathbf{e}}={\boldsymbol{\nu}} in the following. In (110) this just means that we specialize to functions of the form h⁡(𝐱)=h1​(𝐱⋅𝝂)h({\mathbf{x}})=h_{1}({\mathbf{x}}{\cdot}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}) with h1:ℝ→ℝh_{1}:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}. We can therefore carry out the ϕ\phi-integration. The resulting operator will commute with rotations around the 3-axis, so we can express it as a linear combination of operators |m⟩​⟨m|{|m\rangle\langle m|}:

The first line establishes the connection with the premise of Lemma 9: For covariant observables the marginals can be simulated by an exact measurement of mm, with a post-processing kernel PP. Therefore, for covariant FF we have Dmax​(F)=Δmax​(F)D_{\rm max}(F)=\Delta_{\rm max}(F). Since by Lemma 10 the infimum of this quantity, say Δmin​(s)\Delta_{\rm min}(s), is the same as the minimization over all observables. Therefore we can state the measurement uncertainty in the forms

Dmax​(F)≥Δmin​(s)and Δmax​(F)≥Δmin​(s)D_{\rm max}(F)\geq\Delta_{\rm min}(s)\quad\text{and }\quad\Delta_{\rm max}(F)\geq\Delta_{\rm min}(s) (112)

for all observables FF, whether covariant or not. We will now compute Δmin​(s)\Delta_{\rm min}(s), and show that both minima are attained for a unique covariant observable.

IV.5 Minimal Uncertainty

While the above holds for arbitrary exponent α\alpha, we will now restrict to the standard variance case, i.e. α=2\alpha=2.

We will use this Lemma to simplify the minimization over mm. Theorem 12.

The minimal measurement uncertainty Δmin​(s)\Delta_{\rm min}(s) in the sense of (112) is attained at a unique covariant observable, for which Fn​(d​r)F_{n}(dr) is a point measure at n=sn=s and r=rminr=r_{\rm min}, with

(127)

Except for s=1s=1, the maximum over mm in (114) is trivial for the optimal observable, i.e., the calibration error is the same for all calibration inputs mm.

V Conclusions and Outlook

Uncertainty relations can be built for any collection of observables. In this paper we provided some methods, which work in a general setting, but chiefly looked at angular momentum as one of the paradigmatic cases of non-commutativity in quantum mechanics.

The basic mathematical methods are well-developed for the case of preparation uncertainty, so that even in a general case the optimal tradeoff curves can be generated efficiently. We resorted to numerics quite often, since it turns out that the salient optimization problems can rarely be solved analytically for general ss. One of the features one might hope to settle analytically in the future is the asymptotic estimate c2​(s)∝s2/3c_{2}(s)\propto s^{2/3} which comes out with a precision that suggests an exact result.

Much is left to be done for entropic uncertainty. Here we gave only some basic comparisons to the variance case. It would be interesting to see whether the entropic relations can be refined to the point that they can be used to derive sharp variance inequalities as Hirschman did in the phase space case [10].

For measurement uncertainty the general situation is not so favourable, perhaps due to the much more recent introduction of the subject. At this point we know of no efficient way to derive sharp bounds for generic pairs of observables. Nevertheless, we were able to treat the case of a joint measurement of all components in arbitrary directions, because in this case rotational symmetry is not broken and leads to considerable simplification. One of these simplifications is the observation that the two basic error criteria, namely metric uncertainty and calibration error lead to the same results. This was already familiar from the phase space case. However, a further simplification one might have expected from this analogy definitely does not hold: There seems to be no quantitative link between preparation and measurement uncertainty for angular momentum. Further research will show whether useful general connections between the two faces of the uncertainty coin can be established.

The limit large s→∞s\to\infty can be understood as a mean field limit [24], when the spin-ss representation is considered as 2​s2s copies of a spin-1/21/2 system in a symmetric state. We can also see this as a classical limit ℏ→0\hbar\to 0 [34], in the sense that the angular momentum in physical units, i.e., ℏ\hbar is fixed, and hence the dimensionless half-integral representation parameter ss has to diverge. This offers a way to treat not just the uncertainty aspects of this limit, but also the limit of the whole theory of angular momentum.
